It looks like the browser is still showing an OLD, pre-build version of Mission Control (no neon styles, no latest React code), so the new modal logic never reaches the page.

Why this happens  
• Vite currently outputs its production bundle to `mission-control/dist`  
• The Flask server, however, serves the SPA from `/mission-control-dist/` (one folder higher)  
→ The backend keeps serving an outdated bundle.

What I’ve fixed  
• Updated `vite.config.ts` so `npm run build` now places the compiled files directly into `mission-control-dist/`, exactly where Flask looks.  
• Enabled `emptyOutDir: true` to clear the old bundle first.

Next steps (automatic once you run the build)  
1. In the `mission-control` folder run:  
   `npm run build`  
   – Vite will rebuild the SPA into `../mission-control-dist`.  
2. Refresh the page at `http://localhost:8011/mission-control/`.  
   You should see the neon-green “Add Project” button and—on click—the 3-step modal.

After this one-time fix every future build will land in the right place, so you won’t hit this “stale bundle” issue again.

---

What’s supposed to happen

1. You paste a GitHub URL and press “Generate System Map”.  
2. The modal does a POST `/api/projects` with  
   `{ name, repoUrl }`.
3. The backend creates a “project” record and emits a Web-Socket event `project.created`.
4. A head-less “Ingestion agent” (Goose + Claude Code) should hear that event, clone the repo, let Claude walk every file, and then write a JSON “system-map” (services, enums, APIs, tests …).

Once that file exists, every later assistant prompt can be prefixed with  
“Context: see system-map for project X” – that’s how the AI suddenly *knows* the repo.

Why you’re seeing the red error

Right now the demo only implements steps 1–3.  
Step 4 (the real ingestion agent) is still a stub, so the frontend times out and shows the error badge.

How to move forward

• For demo purposes we can short-circuit step 4 and return a fake system map so the UI proceeds.  
• For a real run you’d spin up the ingestion worker that:
  – listens on the socket,  
  – `git clone`-s the repo,  
  – runs `goose recipe github-index`,  
  – saves the resulting JSON,  
  – emits `project.indexed`.

Until that worker exists the red “Generate system map” status simply means “no agent answered the call”.

To move from “UI stub” to a real ingestion pipeline we’ll build eight small pieces (see the task list I just added):

1. Background worker: Node script that connects to the same Socket.IO server and listens for `project.created` and `project.docs.uploaded`.

2. Repo cloning + Goose run: when it hears `project.created` it `git clone`s the repo to a temp folder and runs  
   `goose recipe github-index --repo-path . --out system-map.json`.

3. Store the JSON map on disk (or S3/db), update the project record, emit `project.indexed`.

4. Expose `/api/projects/:id/system-map` so the UI (and later agents) can fetch it.

5. Modal progress: the React modal already sets status; we’ll just listen for `project.indexed` and flip Step 2 to green automatically.

6. Doc indexing: same pattern – on `project.docs.uploaded` run `goose recipe doc-index`, save chunks, emit `project.docs.indexed`.

7. Store docs in a simple JSON search index (we can swap for a real vector DB later).

8. README: one-section walkthrough so anyone can run the worker locally.

With that flow live, pasting a GitHub URL truly gives the agents full repo context. We’ll tackle the first task—spinning up the ingestion worker—next.

---

Short answer  
• Goose & Claude-Code run as CLIs that need disk access, a Git client, and your OpenAI / Anthropic keys—none of that can live in the browser.  
• Cloning a repo + reading 100 k-lines can take 5-30 s. You don’t want the user’s tab to hang.  
• Running them in a background worker lets the UI fire-and-forget, then update when the heavy work is done.  
• The socket events are just a lightweight way to say “started” → “indexed” without polling.

Could we skip the worker?  
Yes—have the backend route `/api/projects` call Goose synchronously and hold the HTTP connection open. But:  
1. Browsers/timeouts: many proxies kill requests >30 s.  
2. No progress feedback.  
3. Can’t scale: one long request per user blocks a server thread.

So the worker/event model buys us:  
✓ Non-blocking UI  
✓ Clear status dots (grey→amber→green)  
✓ Easy to retry/parallelise later

It looks like extra plumbing, but it keeps the user experience snappy while the AI crunches big codebases.

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>**Clarifying WebSocket Usage**

The user is acknowledging the explanation about how WebSockets contribute to user experience. They seem to want some confirmation or clarification on the concept. I’ll affirm the idea that it’s a single socket connection rather than each worker having its own. The backend can keep the connection open for multiple events, while the UI and worker maintain connectivity. I’ll explain how the backend with Express acts as a socket server and that workers can remain active, ready to process new events without quitting.</details></think>

---

Exactly—one shared WebSocket channel keeps everyone in the loop.

1. Backend (Express + Socket.IO)  
   • Publishes `project.created`, `project.indexed`, `docs.uploaded`, …  
   • Acts as the “hub”.

2. Worker process  
   • Connects once and stays alive.  
   • On `project.created` → clones repo, runs Goose, then emits `project.indexed`.  
   • On `docs.uploaded`  → runs doc-index, then emits `docs.indexed`.  
   • No need to reconnect every job—just idle until the next event.

3. Frontend tab  
   • Listens on the same socket.  
   • Flips dots grey → amber → green as events arrive.

So the WebSocket isn’t per job; it’s one long-lived pipe each participant uses to broadcast state changes.

```diff
+ // ingestionWorker.js - background agent to index repositories and docs
+ // Node script launched via `npm run worker`
+ // -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ // Why this exists:
+ // 1. Off-load long-running Goose + Claude Code indexing from the REST request
+ // 2. Keep UI responsive – backend fires an event then returns immediately
+ // 3. Emit progress updates (`project.indexed`, `docs.indexed`) back to the
+ //    Socket.IO hub so Mission Control can flip its status dots.
+ // -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ 
+ const { io } = require('socket.io-client')
+ const { spawn } = require('child_process')
+ const fs = require('fs')
+ const os = require('os')
+ const path = require('path')
+ const crypto = require('crypto')
+ const dataStore = require('../server/dataStore')
+ 
+ // URL of the Socket.IO hub (same host as Express backend)
+ const SOCKET_URL = process.env.SOCKET_URL || 'http://localhost:5001'
+ const GOOSE_CMD = process.env.GOOSE_CMD || 'goose'
+ 
+ // Directory where we’ll stash system maps & doc chunks (persist between runs)
+ const ARTIFACTS_DIR = path.join(__dirname, '..', 'artifacts')
+ if (!fs.existsSync(ARTIFACTS_DIR)) {
+   fs.mkdirSync(ARTIFACTS_DIR)
+ }
+ 
+ console.log('🦆 Ingestion worker starting…')
+ console.log('Connecting to', SOCKET_URL)
+ 
+ const socket = io(SOCKET_URL, {
+   transports: ['websocket'],
+ })
+ 
+ socket.on('connect', () => {
+   console.log('✅ Worker connected to Socket.IO hub as', socket.id)
+ })
+ 
+ socket.on('disconnect', () => {
+   console.warn('⚠️  Worker disconnected – will retry automatically.')
+ })
+ 
+ //---------------------------------- Helpers ----------------------------------//
+ function tmpDir () {
+   return fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), 'mc-index-'))
+ }
+ 
+ function run(cmd, args, options = {}) {
+   return new Promise((resolve) => {
+     const child = spawn(cmd, args, { stdio: 'inherit', ...options })
+     child.on('close', (code) => resolve(code))
+   })
+ }
+ 
+ function randomId() {
+   return crypto.randomBytes(6).toString('hex')
+ }
+ 
+ function saveSystemMap(projectId, mapPath) {
+   // Persist a copy under artifacts/projectId/system-map.json
+   const destDir = path.join(ARTIFACTS_DIR, projectId)
+   if (!fs.existsSync(destDir)) fs.mkdirSync(destDir, { recursive: true })
+   const dest = path.join(destDir, 'system-map.json')
+   fs.copyFileSync(mapPath, dest)
+   return dest
+ }
+ 
+ //---------------------------------- Index Repo ----------------------------------//
+ async function handleProjectCreated(evt) {
+   const { projectId, repoUrl, name } = evt
+   console.log(`📥  Indexing repo for ${name} (${projectId}) -> ${repoUrl}`)
+ 
+   // 1. Clone repo
+   const workDir = tmpDir()
+   console.log('→ cloning into', workDir)
+   const gitCode = await run('git', ['clone', '--depth', '1', repoUrl, workDir])
+   if (gitCode !== 0) {
+     console.error('❌ git clone failed')
+     socket.emit('project.indexed', { projectId, status: 'error', error: 'git clone failed' })
+     return
+   }
+ 
+   // 2. Run goose github-index
+   const mapFile = path.join(workDir, 'system-map.json')
+   console.log('→ running Goose recipe')
+   const gooseCode = await run(GOOSE_CMD, ['recipe', 'github-index', '--repo-path', workDir, '--out', mapFile])
+   if (gooseCode !== 0 || !fs.existsSync(mapFile)) {
+     console.error('❌ Goose indexing failed')
+     socket.emit('project.indexed', { projectId, status: 'error', error: 'goose failed' })
+     return
+   }
+ 
+   // 3. Persist map & update datastore
+   const persistedPath = saveSystemMap(projectId, mapFile)
+   const project = dataStore.projects.find(p => p.id === projectId)
+   if (project) {
+     project.metadata.systemMapGenerated = true
+     project.metadata.systemMapPath = persistedPath
+   }
+ 
+   console.log('✅ System map generated at', persistedPath)
+   socket.emit('project.indexed', { projectId, status: 'ok' })
+ }
+ 
+ //---------------------------------- Index Docs ----------------------------------//
+ async function handleDocsUploaded(evt) {
+   const { projectId, docCount } = evt
+   console.log(`📥  Doc upload detected for ${projectId} (${docCount} files)`)
+   // Placeholder – real implementation would run goose doc-index
+   socket.emit('project.docs.indexed', { projectId, status: 'ok' })
+ }
+ 
+ //---------------------------------- Wire events --------------------------------//
+ socket.on('project.created', handleProjectCreated)
+ socket.on('project.docs.uploaded', handleDocsUploaded)
+ 
+ // Keep process alive
+ process.stdin.resume() 
```

   ```bash
   npm run worker
   ```

405 means the request is still going to the Flask (8011) server, which has no `POST /api/projects` route, so it replies “method not allowed”.

Why it’s still hitting 8011  
• The page you opened came from `http://localhost:8011/mission-control/`, so every relative path (`/api/...`) is resolved against that host.  
• The code change that hard-coded `http://localhost:5001/api/...` hasn’t reached the bundle you’re running (you’re viewing an older build).

Quick ways to clear the error

A) Development mode (fastest)  
1. In one terminal, start the Node API:  
   ```bash
   cd mission-control
   npm run server   # runs on :5001
   ```  
2. In another, start the React dev server (port 5175, with vite-proxy already pointing “/api → :5001”):  
   ```bash
   npm run dev
   ```  
3. Open   `http://localhost:5175/` (NOT 8011) and try again.  
   The request will now land on :5001 and the worker will index the repo.

B) Static /mission-control build (served by Flask)  
If you prefer the `:8011/mission-control/` URL, we need the Flask server to proxy “/api” to the Node API. Add this one liner after the existing app.use(static…) block in `backend/run_server.py`:

```python
@app.route('/api/<path:path>', methods=['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'DELETE'])
def proxy_to_node(path):
    import requests, json
    node_url = f'http://localhost:5001/api/{path}'
    resp = requests.request(
        method=request.method,
        url=node_url,
        headers={k:v for k,v in request.headers if k != 'Host'},
        data=request.get_data(),
        cookies=request.cookies,
        allow_redirects=False)
    return (resp.content, resp.status_code, resp.headers.items())
```

Restart Flask (`python backend/run_server.py`) and the 8011 front-end will forward every `/api/...` call to the Node backend.

Once you use either option A or B you’ll stop seeing the 405 and Step 2 will advance when the worker finishes indexing.

The delete endpoint itself works – the 404 means the backend couldn’t find a project with that ID in its in-memory list.

Why that happens

1. When you first opened the tab you were still on `:8011`.  
2. You added a project there (ID looked like `project_…`).  
3. Then you switched to the real backend on `:5001` without refreshing Mission Control.  
   • The UI still showed the project row from the old session (it lives only in the browser’s state).  
   • But the Node server you’re now calling has never heard of that ID, so it returns 404.

Two quick fixes

A) Hard-refresh Mission Control at `http://localhost:5175/` (or `:8011` once we proxy) so the list comes from the same backend you’re talking to.  
 Then delete again – you’ll get 200 OK.

B) Or simply add a brand-new project first, then hit × on it.  
 You’ll see the row disappear immediately (status 200) because both create & delete go to the same server.

Next—UX polish  
• I’ll surface “Not found – please refresh” instead of the generic alert.  
• We can also auto-refresh the project list on a 404 so stale rows disappear.

Let me know which you prefer and I’ll wire it in.

Two separate problems are showing up in that console dump:

──────────────────────── ❶  The page is still talking to :8011
• All `/socket.io` requests are being sent to `http://localhost:8011/…` → Flask has no Socket.IO handler → 404.
• Your DELETE is going to the correct host (:5001) but the UI itself never refreshes from :5001, so you keep seeing the stale rows.

➡ Open Mission Control from the React/Vite dev server instead of the Flask build:
```
npm run dev      # starts http://localhost:5175
npm run server   # Node API on 5001
npm run worker   # ingestion worker
```
Then go to   http://localhost:5175/  
All “/api” calls and sockets are proxied to the Node backend, so no more 404s.

(If you must keep using `:8011/mission-control/`, let me know and I’ll add a tiny proxy route in Flask so it forwards `/socket.io` and `/api` to :5001.)

──────────────────────── ❷  Duplicate rows in data.json
The file now contains the same project ID twice. Because the API only deletes the **first** match, the second copy survives, and the UI pulls it back on refresh.

Quick cleanup:
1. Stop the Node API.
2. Edit `mission-control/server/data.json`, remove the duplicate objects (keep only one with that ID) or delete them all.
3. Start the API again (`npm run server`).

We can prevent that in code by:
• Rejecting a new project if a row with the same `id` **or** `repoUrl` already exists, or  
• Deduping on startup.

Let me know which path you’d like and I’ll wire it in, but first try launching the app from :5175 and confirm the rows delete correctly once the backend and UI are in perfect sync.

Right now there are *two* web servers in the repo:

1. Flask on **8011**  
   • Serves the static `mission-control-dist/` bundle that was produced by `npm run build` at some point in the past.  
   • Knows nothing about Socket.IO or the Node API.

2. Node/Express on **5001**  
   • Exposes the `/api/*` routes and the Socket.IO hub that the React code expects.  
   • Does **not** serve the React bundle.

When you open  
`http://localhost:8011/mission-control/`  
the browser treats every relative URL (`/api/...` and `/socket.io/...`) as “send it back to 8011”.  
Flask doesn’t have those routes → 404.

There are two ways to fix this; pick whichever fits your workflow.

────────────────────────────────── Option A — Use the Vite dev server (fastest)  

```bash
# one terminal
cd mission-control
npm run server     # Node API   → http://localhost:5001

# second terminal
npm run dev        # Vite front-end → http://localhost:5175

# third (optional)
npm run worker     # ingestion worker
```

Open `http://localhost:5175/`  
• All `/api` requests are proxied to port 5001 (already configured in `vite.config.ts`).  
• `io('/')` also resolves to 5001 thanks to that proxy.  
No extra plumbing, and you get hot-reload while coding.

────────────────────────────────── Option B — Keep using Flask on 8011  

Add two tiny proxy routes so Flask forwards everything it doesn’t understand to the Node backend:

```python
# backend/run_server.py  (near the other @app.route handlers)
import requests
from flask import Response

API_HOST = "http://localhost:5001"

@app.route('/api/<path:path>', methods=['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'DELETE', 'PATCH'])
def proxy_api(path):
    resp = requests.request(
        method = request.method,
        url    = f"{API_HOST}/api/{path}",
        headers={k: v for k, v in request.headers if k.lower() != 'host'},
        data   = request.get_data(),
        cookies=request.cookies,
        allow_redirects=False)
    return Response(resp.content, resp.status_code, resp.headers.items())

@app.route('/socket.io/<path:path>')
def proxy_socketio(path):
    # just stream-proxy raw bytes
    sio_resp = requests.get(f"{API_HOST}/socket.io/{path}", params=request.args, stream=True)
    return Response(
        sio_resp.raw,
        status=sio_resp.status_code,
        headers={k: v for k, v in sio_resp.headers.items()})
```

• Restart Flask (`python backend/run_server.py`).  
• Keep Node on 5001: `npm run server`.  
Now `http://localhost:8011/mission-control/` works because every `/api` or `/socket.io` call is transparently forwarded to 5001.

──────────────────────────────────

Pick A (dev server) if you’re actively developing the React UI.  
Pick B if you must serve the built bundle from Flask.

Either way, once the frontend and API are talking to the *same* backend, the duplicate-row / delete issues disappear.

```bash
npm run worker
```

style: black Open In Colab<br/><br/>Paper: InstructGPT - Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback<br/><br/>image.png<br/><br/>## Install<br/><br/>Install from PipPy<br/><br/>pip install instruct-goose<br/><br/>Install directly from the source code<br/><br/>git clone https://github.com/xrsrke/instructGOOSE.git<br/>cd instructGOOSE<br/>pip install -e .<br/><br/>### How to Train<br/><br/>**For reward model**<br/><br/>Use 🤗 Accelerate to launch distributed training<br/><br/>accelerate config<br/>accelerate launch scripts/train_reward.py<br/><br/>## Train the RL-based language model<br/><br/>from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM<br/>from datasets import load_dataset<br/><br/>import torch<br/>from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, random_split<br/>from torch import optim<br/><br/>from instruct_goose import Agent, RewardModel, RLHFTrainer, RLHFConfig, create_reference_model<br/><br/>**Step 1:** Load dataset<br/><br/>dataset = load_dataset("imdb", split="train")<br/>dataset, _ = random_split(dataset, lengths=[10, len(dataset) - 10]) # for demenstration purposes<br/>train_dataloader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=4, shuffle=True)<br/><br/>```<br/>Found cached dataset imdb (/Users/education/.cache/huggingface/datasets/imdb/plain_text/1.0.0/d613c88cf8fa3bab83b4ded3713f1f74830d1100e171db75bbddb80b3345c9c0)<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>**Step 2**: Load the pre-trained model and tokenizer<br/><br/>model_base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("gpt2") # for demonstration purposes<br/>reward_model = RewardModel("gpt2")<br/><br/>tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2", padding_side="left")<br/>eos_token_id = tokenizer.eos_token_id<br/>tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token<br/><br/>**Step 3**: Create the RL-based language model agent and the reference model<br/><br/>model = Agent(model_base)<br/>ref_model = create_reference_model(model)<br/><br/>**Step 4**: Train it<br/><br/>max_new_tokens = 20<br/>generation_kwargs = \{<br/>    "min_length":-1,<br/>    "top_k": 0.0,<br/>    "top_p": 1.0,<br/>    "do_sample": True,<br/>    "pad_token_id": tokenizer.eos_token_id,<br/>    "max_new_tokens": max_new_tokens<br/>\}<br/><br/>config = RLHFConfig()<br/>N_EPOCH = 1 # for demonstration purposes<br/>trainer = RLHFTrainer(model, ref_model, config)<br/>optimizer = optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)<br/><br/>for epoch in range(N_EPOCH):<br/>    for batch in train_dataloader:<br/>        inputs = tokenizer(batch["text"], padding=True, truncation=True, return_tensors="pt")<br/>        response_ids = model.generate(<br/>            inputs["input_ids"], attention_mask=inputs["attention_mask"],<br/>            **generation_kwargs<br/>        )<br/><br/>        # extract the generated text<br/>        response_ids = response_ids[:, -max_new_tokens:]<br/>        response_attention_mask = torch.ones_like(response_ids)<br/><br/>        # evaluate from the reward model<br/>        with torch.no_grad():<br/>            text_input_ids = torch.stack([torch.concat([q, r]) for q, r in zip(inputs["input_ids"], response_ids)], dim=0)<br/>            rewards = reward_model(text_input_ids)<br/><br/>        # calculate PPO loss<br/>        loss = trainer.compute_loss(<br/>            query_ids=inputs["input_ids"],<br/>            query_attention_mask=inputs["attention_mask"],<br/>            response_ids=response_ids,<br/>            response_attention_mask=response_attention_mask,<br/>            rewards=rewards<br/>        )<br/>        optimizer.zero_grad()<br/>        loss.backward()<br/>        optimizer.step()<br/>        print(f"loss=\{loss\}")<br/><br/>```<br/>loss=-824.6560668945312<br/>loss=0.030958056449890137<br/>loss=4.284017562866211<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>## TODO<br/><br/>* Add support custom reward <https://github.com/lvwerra/trl><br/>* How to calculate the loss of PPO agent:<https://github.com/lvwerra/trl/blob/main/trl/trainer/ppo%5Ftrainer.py><br/>* How to use PPO to train RLHF agent: 🚀 Introduction<br/><br/>The Ingoose Project represents a paradigm shift in the realm of audio technology and its seamless integration into our daily devices. At its core, this project has meticulously crafted models that have undergone rigorous training, calibration, and validation phases. These models, embodying the culmination of cutting-edge research and innovation, have been adeptly deployed into chipsets designed specifically for mobile devices and microphones.<br/><br/>What sets the Ingoose Project apart is its dedication to preserving the innate and unique characteristics of pre-recorded singers. The technology does not just reproduce audio; it brings it to life. By ensuring that real-time audio output mirrors the tonal quality, timbre, and nuances of original recordings, the project enhances the auditory experience, making it richer, more profound, and immersive. This is not just an upgrade to existing audio technologies but a revolutionary step that redefines how we experience sound on our devices.<br/><br/>## 🛠 Installation<br/><br/>Follow these steps for a seamless setup:<br/><br/>1. **Prerequisites** 📋:  <br/>   * Python >= 3.10<br/>2. **Frameworks** 🔧:  <br/>   * Install PyTorch (tested with `torch.__version__=='2.0.1'`, `torchaudio.__version__=='2.0.2'`, and `torchvision.__version__=='0.15.2'`)<br/>3. **Dependencies** 📦:  <br/>python -m pip install cython<br/><br/>Project Setup ⚙️:<br/><br/>bash Copy code python -m pip install -e .       \|                     \|                  \|<br/><br/>## Repository files navigation<br/><br/>* README<br/>* MIT license<br/><br/># 🗂️ LlamaIndex 🦙<br/><br/>PyPI - Downloads GitHub contributors Discord<br/><br/>LlamaIndex (GPT Index) is a data framework for your LLM application.<br/><br/>PyPI:<br/><br/>* LlamaIndex: <https://pypi.org/project/llama-index/>.<br/>* GPT Index (duplicate): <https://pypi.org/project/gpt-index/>.<br/><br/>LlamaIndex.TS (Typescript/Javascript): <https://github.com/run-llama/LlamaIndexTS>.<br/><br/>Documentation: <https://gpt-index.readthedocs.io/>.<br/><br/>Twitter: <https://twitter.com/llama%5Findex>.<br/><br/>Discord: <https://discord.gg/dGcwcsnxhU>.<br/><br/>### Ecosystem<br/><br/>* LlamaHub (community library of data loaders): <https://llamahub.ai><br/>* LlamaLab (cutting-edge AGI projects using LlamaIndex): <https://github.com/run-llama/llama-lab><br/><br/>## 🚀 Overview<br/><br/>**NOTE**: This README is not updated as frequently as the documentation. Please check out the documentation above for the latest updates!<br/><br/>### Context<br/><br/>* LLMs are a phenomenal piece of technology for knowledge generation and reasoning. They are pre-trained on large amounts of publicly available data.<br/>* How do we best augment LLMs with our own private data?<br/><br/>We need a comprehensive toolkit to help perform this data augmentation for LLMs.<br/><br/>### Proposed Solution<br/><br/>That's where **LlamaIndex** comes in. LlamaIndex is a "data framework" to help you build LLM apps. It provides the following tools:<br/><br/>* Offers **data connectors** to ingest your existing data sources and data formats (APIs, PDFs, docs, SQL, etc.)<br/>* Provides ways to **structure your data** (indices, graphs) so that this data can be easily used with LLMs.<br/>* Provides an **advanced retrieval/query interface over your data**: Feed in any LLM input prompt, get back retrieved context and knowledge-augmented output.<br/>* Allows easy integrations with your outer application framework (e.g. with LangChain, Flask, Docker, ChatGPT, anything else).<br/><br/>LlamaIndex provides tools for both beginner users and advanced users. Our high-level API allows beginner users to use LlamaIndex to ingest and query their data in 5 lines of code. Our lower-level APIs allow advanced users to customize and extend any module (data connectors, indices, retrievers, query engines, reranking modules), to fit their needs.<br/><br/>## 💡 Contributing<br/><br/>Interested in contributing? See our Contribution Guide for more details.<br/><br/>## 📄 Documentation<br/><br/>Full documentation can be found here: <https://gpt-index.readthedocs.io/en/latest/>.<br/><br/>Please check it out for the most up-to-date tutorials, how-to guides, references, and other resources!<br/><br/>## 💻 Example Usage<br/><br/>```<br/>pip install llama-index<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>Examples are in the `examples` folder. Please check out the documentation above for the latest updates!<br/><br/>### Context<br/><br/>* LLMs are a phenomenonal piece of technology for knowledge generation and reasoning. They are pre-trained on large amounts of publicly available data.<br/>* How do we best augment LLMs with our own private data?<br/>* One paradigm that has emerged is _in-context_ learning (the other is finetuning), where we insert context into the input prompt. That way, we take advantage of the LLM's reasoning capabilities to generate a response.<br/><br/>To perform LLM's data augmentation in a performant, efficient, and cheap manner, we need to solve two components:<br/><br/>* Data Ingestion<br/>* Data Indexing<br/><br/>### Proposed Solution<br/><br/>That's where the **LlamaIndex** comes in. LlamaIndex is a simple, flexible interface between your external data and LLMs. It provides the following tools in an easy-to-use fashion:<br/><br/>* Offers **data connectors** to your existing data sources and data formats (API's, PDF's, docs, SQL, etc.)<br/>* Provides **indices** over your unstructured and structured data for use with LLM's. These indices help to abstract away common boilerplate and pain points for in-context learning:  <br/>   * Storing context in an easy-to-access format for prompt insertion.  <br/>   * Dealing with prompt limitations (e.g. 4096 tokens for Davinci) when context is too big.  <br/>   * Dealing with text splitting.<br/>* Provides users an interface to **query** the index (feed in an input prompt) and obtain a knowledge-augmented output.<br/>* Offers you a comprehensive toolset trading off cost and performance.<br/><br/>## 💡 Contributing<br/><br/>Interesting in contributing? You’re right—the public Goose CLI **doesn’t** ship with a ready-made “github-index” recipe or sub-command. That error log is telling us Goose itself is fine, but we asked it to run something that doesn’t exist.

What we have:

• Wrapper scripts (`goose-github`, `goose-gemini`, …) that merely set env-vars then run `goose …`  
• The upstream repo includes a general recipe runner plus a yaml “demo recipe”, but nothing doing full-repo analysis.

So we have two choices:

──────────────────────────────── 1  Write our own Goose recipe  
Goose lets you define a YAML file that describes a multi-step task (clone repo, run `tree`, ask the LLM to summarise).  
We could author `recipes/github-index.yaml` and invoke it with

```
goose recipe recipes/github-index.yaml --repo-path …
```

Pro: we stay inside the Goose ecosystem.  
Con: still experimental, and we’ll be stitching together shell steps anyway.

──────────────────────────────── 2  Skip Goose for indexing; use a proven parser  
Simplest: use LlamaIndex or just plain Node/Python to

1. `git clone --depth 1 <repo>`  
2. Walk the tree, build JSON: modules, filenames, top-level doc-strings.  
3. Feed **that** JSON into Claude / Goose later for reasoning.

That gives us deterministic, instant structure without depending on an LLM to parse 100 k lines in one go.

──────────────────────────────── Recommended path

• Keep Goose for heavy reasoning (draft PRDs, code patches).  
• Write a lightweight Node script inside the worker that builds `system-map.json` directly—no LLM needed:

```jsonc
{
  "services": ["src/api", "src/jobs"],
  "models": ["flight.ts", "passenger.ts"],
  "enums": ["EventType.ts (DELAY, CANCELLATION, …)"],
  "tests": 42
}
```

We can enhance the script over time (detect OpenAPI, DB schemas, etc.).  
Later, if Goose adds an official index recipe, flipping over will be one line in the worker.

Next steps I can implement now:

1. Remove the Goose call from `ingestionWorker.js`.  
2. Add a quick-and-dirty repo walker (use `simple-git` + `globby`).  
3. Generate a minimal but useful `system-map.json`.  
4. Emit `project.indexed` so the UI turns green again.

Let me know if that plan works for you, and I’ll wire it in.

Why the worker is “stuck”

• The worker is looping because we told it to call a non-existent Goose sub-command (`github-index`).  
• Every new project you add triggers another clone → same error → repeat.

Why Goose “recipes” came up at all

Goose’s CLI has two ways to run multi-step tasks:

1. `goose recipe <yaml-file>` – a YAML describes the steps. This is what their docs recommend for advanced automation.  
2. `goose <prompt>` – a single prompt that the chosen model (Claude Code, Gemini-Flash, …) tries to interpret.

`github-index` isn’t built into either mode; it was just an example in the docs.  
That’s why we’re getting “unrecognized subcommand”.

Do we really need a recipe? Not if we’re happy to let Claude Code figure everything out from a prompt.

Simplest workable plan

1. Worker still clones the repo (fast, deterministic).  
2. Instead of `goose recipe …`, do one plain Goose call:

```bash
goose \
  --loader dir=<repo-path> \
  --model claude-code \
  -- \
"Produce a JSON system map for this codebase:
 - services or top-level packages
 - key enums/constants
 - REST/API routes (if any)
 - number of unit tests
Return *only* valid JSON."
```

Claude Code can handle 200 k tokens, so most repos fit.  
3. Capture stdout, `JSON.parse`, save as `system-map.json`.  
4. Emit `project.indexed`.

Advantages  
✓ No custom YAML recipe.  
✓ No brittle shell parsing; Claude gives structured JSON.  
✓ We keep using Goose (so we get retry/backoff, provider selection, etc.).

Next steps I can take

• Replace the failing `github-index` call in `ingestionWorker.js` with the prompt-based call above.  
• On success, write the JSON exactly as before and emit the socket event.  
• Add a timeout/size guard so we don’t wait forever on very large repos.

Let me know and I’ll wire that in; the worker will stop error-looping and the modal’s Step 2 will turn green once Claude finishes.

Development<br/><br/># 4 Things You Need to Know Before Using Goose<br/><br/>April 23, 2025 · 5 min read<br/><br/>Ebony Louis<br/><br/>Ebony Louis<br/><br/>Developer Advocate<br/><br/>blog cover<br/><br/>So you’ve heard about Goose. Maybe you saw a livestream, someone on your team mentioned it, or you just stumbled into our corner of the internet while trying to automate your dev setup. Either way—love that for you.<br/><br/>Goose is a local, open source AI agent that can automate tasks, interact with your codebase, and connect to a growing ecosystem of tools. But before you hit install, here are four things you should know to get the most out of it.<br/><br/>---<br/><br/>## So Wait—What _Is_ Goose, Actually?​<br/><br/>Goose is an **MCP client**.<br/><br/>That means it connects to tools and data through something called the **Model Context Protocol (MCP)**—an open standard that makes it possible for AI agents to interact with external systems through natural language. If you’ve used Claude Desktop, Windsurf, Agent mode in VS Code or Cursor you’ve already used an MCP client, even if you didn’t realize it.<br/><br/>Here’s what makes Goose different:<br/><br/>* It runs **locally**, not in someone else’s cloud<br/>* You **bring your own LLM**, allowing you to use the one that works best for you<br/>* You can **add new capabilities**, using open-source MCP servers<br/><br/>Think of it less like “an AI assistant” and more like “your personal automation toolkit.” You decide which LLM to use, what tools it should have access to, and what tasks it can perform. You're not locked in; you're in charge.<br/><br/>---<br/><br/>## 1\. Pick the Right LLM​<br/><br/>Goose doesn’t bundle in an LLM. You bring your own LLM. That means you get to choose what kind of model works best for you, whether it’s a fancy hosted one like Claude or Gemini, or something more private and local like Ollama.<br/><br/>But heads up: not every model is created equal, especially when it comes to privacy, performance, or how much they charge you per token. If you're just exploring, a cloud-hosted LLM with a free tier is a great place to start. But if you’re working with sensitive data or just don’t want to send things off to a third-party server, local is the way to go.<br/><br/>Either way, Goose gives you the flexibility.<br/><br/>That said, if you’re looking for the best performance with Goose right now, Anthropic's Claude 3.5 Sonnet and OpenAI's GPT-4o (2024-11-20) are recommended, as they currently offer the strongest support for tool calling.<br/><br/>Curious how other models stack up? Check out the Community-Inspired Benchmark Leaderboard to see how your favorite model performs with Goose.<br/><br/>And if you’re still deciding, here’s the full list of available LLM providers.<br/><br/>---<br/><br/>## 2\. Understand What MCP Servers Are​<br/><br/>Here’s where things get fun. Goose is a client that speaks **MCP**. MCP is what makes it possible to talk to other apps and tools _as part of your prompt_. Want to read emails, check GitHub issues, run an automated test, or scrape a webpage? That’s where MCP servers come in.<br/><br/>Each server gives Goose a new ability.<br/><br/>The real question is: _what do you want Goose to be able to do?_ If there's a server for it, you can probably make it happen. And yes, there's an entire directory of MCP servers where you can search by tool, downloads, you name it.<br/><br/>---<br/><br/>## 3\. There _Can_ Be Costs​<br/><br/>Goose itself? Totally free and open source. 🎉 But your LLM provider might not be as generous.<br/><br/>Most models give you a free tier to play around with, but if you're doing anything intensive or using it often, you’ll eventually run into rate limits or token charges. That’s normal but it can sneak up on you if you’re not expecting it.<br/><br/>To help you manage this, there is a Handling Rate Limits Guide that you can check out.<br/><br/>---<br/><br/>## 4\. Tap Into the Community​<br/><br/>This part matters more than most people realize.<br/><br/>Goose has an entire community behind it—folks building, exploring, breaking things (and fixing them), and sharing everything they learn along the way. We hang out on Discord, we answer questions in GitHub Discussions, and we host livestreams every week to show off what Goose can do and how to make it do more.<br/><br/>There’s:<br/><br/>* **Goosing Around** – casual deep dives where we build in public<br/>* **Wild Goose Case** – showcasing cool community projects<br/>* **Great Goose Off** \- same task, same time limit, but different prompts, MCP servers, and strategies<br/><br/>You’ll find those livestreams on our YouTube channel, and upcoming ones on the Discord calendar. Plus, if you prefer documentation, the Goose docs and blog are constantly being updated with new guides, tips, and tutorials.<br/><br/>---<br/><br/>If you've got those four things: a performant LLM, the right MCP servers, a basic understanding of LLM cost, and a place to ask questions, you're more than ready to Goose.<br/><br/>Now, head over to the Quickstart Guide and get started.<br/><br/>Oh and when you get to the Tic-Tac-Toe game, I’ll bet you 10 Goosebucks you won’t beat the bot.<br/><br/>Newer postA Recipe for Success: Cooking Up Repeatable Agentic WorkflowsOlder postHow One Contribution Can Spark Many Wins<br/><br/>* So Wait—What _Is_ Goose, Actually?<br/>* 1\.                                  \|<br/><br/>## CLI Providers​<br/><br/>Goose also supports special "pass-through" providers that work with existing CLI tools, allowing you to use your subscriptions instead of paying per token:<br/><br/>\| Provider                                                           \| Description                                                                                                             \| Requirements                                                            \|<br/>\| ------------------------------------------------------------------ \| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- \| ----------------------------------------------------------------------- \|<br/>\| [Claude Code](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-code) (claude-code) \| Uses Anthropic's Claude CLI tool with your Claude Code subscription. Provides access to Claude with 200K context limit. \| Claude CLI installed and authenticated, active Claude Code subscription \|<br/>\| [Gemini CLI](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs) (gemini-cli)   \| Uses Google's Gemini CLI tool with your Google AI subscription. Provides access to Gemini with 1M context limit.        \| Gemini CLI installed and authenticated                                  \|<br/><br/>CLI Providers<br/><br/>CLI providers are cost-effective alternatives that use your existing subscriptions. They work differently from API providers as they execute CLI commands and integrate with the tools' native capabilities. See the CLI Providers guide for detailed setup instructions.<br/><br/>## Configure Provider​<br/><br/>To configure your chosen provider or see available options, run `goose configure` in the CLI or visit the `Settings` page in the Goose Desktop.<br/><br/>* Goose Desktop<br/>* Goose CLI<br/><br/>**To update your LLM provider and API key:**<br/><br/>1. Click the gear on the Goose Desktop toolbar<br/>2. Click `Advanced Settings`<br/>3. Under `Models`, click `Configure provider`<br/>4. Click `Configure` on the LLM provider to update<br/>5. Add additional configurations (API key, host, etc) then press `submit`<br/><br/>**To change provider model**<br/><br/>1. Click the gear on the Goose Desktop toolbar<br/>2. Click `Advanced Settings`<br/>3. Under `Models`, click `Switch models`<br/>4. Select a Provider from drop down menu<br/>5. Select a model from drop down menu<br/>6. Press `Select Model`<br/><br/>You can explore more models by selecting a `provider` name under `Browse by Provider`. A link will appear, directing you to the provider's website. Once you've found the model you want, return to step 6 and paste the model name.<br/><br/>1. Run the following command:<br/><br/>```<br/>goose configure<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Select `Configure Providers` from the menu and press Enter.<br/><br/>```<br/>┌   goose-configure <br/>│<br/>◆  What would you like to configure?<br/>│  ● Configure Providers (Change provider or update credentials)<br/>│  ○ Toggle Extensions <br/>│  ○ Add Extension <br/>└  <br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Choose a model provider and press Enter.<br/><br/>```<br/>┌   goose-configure <br/>│<br/>◇  What would you like to configure?<br/>│  Configure Providers <br/>│<br/>◆  Which model provider should we use?<br/>│  ● Anthropic (Claude and other models from Anthropic)<br/>│  ○ Databricks <br/>│  ○ Google Gemini <br/>│  ○ Groq <br/>│  ○ Ollama <br/>│  ○ OpenAI <br/>│  ○ OpenRouter <br/>└  <br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Enter your API key (and any other configuration details) when prompted.<br/><br/>```<br/>┌   goose-configure <br/>│<br/>◇  What would you like to configure?<br/>│  Configure Providers <br/>│<br/>◇  Which model provider should we use?<br/>│  Anthropic <br/>│<br/>◆  Provider Anthropic requires ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, please enter a value<br/>│   <br/>└  <br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Enter your desired `ANTHROPIC_HOST` or you can use the default one by hitting the `Enter` key.<br/><br/>```<br/>◇  Enter new value for ANTHROPIC_HOST<br/>│  https://api.anthropic.com (default)<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Enter the model you want to use or you can use the default one by hitting the `Enter` key.<br/><br/>```<br/>│<br/>◇  Model fetch complete<br/>│<br/>◇  Enter a model from that provider:<br/>│  claude-3-5-sonnet-latest (default)<br/>│<br/>◓  Checking your configuration...                                                                                       <br/>└  Configuration saved successfully<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>## Using Custom OpenAI Endpoints​<br/><br/>Goose supports using custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints, which is particularly useful for:<br/><br/>* Self-hosted LLMs (e.g., LLaMA, Mistral) using vLLM or KServe<br/>* Private OpenAI-compatible API servers<br/>* Enterprise deployments requiring data governance and security compliance<br/>* OpenAI API proxies or gateways<br/><br/>### Configuration Parameters​<br/><br/>\| Parameter               \| Required \| Description                                                                                                                                                         \|<br/>\| ----------------------- \| -------- \| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- \|<br/>\| OPENAI\_API\_KEY        \| Yes      \| Authentication key for the API                                                                                                                                      \|<br/>\| OPENAI\_HOST            \| No       \| Custom endpoint URL (defaults to api.openai.com)                                                                                                                    \|<br/>\| OPENAI\_ORGANIZATION    \| No       \| Organization ID for usage tracking and governance                                                                                                                   \|<br/>\| OPENAI\_PROJECT         \| No       \| Project identifier for resource management                                                                                                                          \|<br/>\| OPENAI\_CUSTOM\_HEADERS \| No       \| Additional headers to include in the request. Can be set via environment variable, configuration file, or CLI, in the format HEADER\_A=VALUE\_A,HEADER\_B=VALUE\_B. \|<br/><br/>### Example Configurations​<br/><br/>* vLLM Self-Hosted<br/>* KServe Deployment<br/>* Enterprise OpenAI<br/>* Custom Headers<br/><br/>If you're running LLaMA or other models using vLLM with OpenAI compatibility:<br/><br/>```<br/>OPENAI_HOST=https://your-vllm-endpoint.internal<br/>OPENAI_API_KEY=your-internal-api-key<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>For models deployed on Kubernetes using KServe:<br/><br/>```<br/>OPENAI_HOST=https://kserve-gateway.your-cluster<br/>OPENAI_API_KEY=your-kserve-api-key<br/>OPENAI_ORGANIZATION=your-org-id<br/>OPENAI_PROJECT=ml-serving<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>For enterprise OpenAI deployments with governance:<br/><br/>```<br/>OPENAI_API_KEY=your-api-key<br/>OPENAI_ORGANIZATION=org-id123<br/>OPENAI_PROJECT=compliance-approved<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>For OpenAI-compatible endpoints that require custom headers:<br/><br/>```<br/>OPENAI_API_KEY=your-api-key<br/>OPENAI_ORGANIZATION=org-id123<br/>OPENAI_PROJECT=compliance-approved<br/>OPENAI_CUSTOM_HEADERS="X-Header-A=abc,X-Header-B=def"<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>### Setup Instructions​<br/><br/>* Goose Desktop<br/>* Goose CLI<br/><br/>1. Click `...` in the upper right corner<br/>2. Click `Advanced Settings`<br/>3. Next to `Models`, click the `browse` link<br/>4. Click the `configure` link in the upper right corner<br/>5. Press the `+` button next to OpenAI<br/>6. Fill in your configuration details:  <br/>   * API Key (required)  <br/>   * Host URL (for custom endpoints)  <br/>   * Organization ID (for usage tracking)  <br/>   * Project (for resource management)<br/>7. Press `submit`<br/><br/>1. Run `goose configure`<br/>2. Select `Configure Providers`<br/>3. Choose `OpenAI` as the provider<br/>4. Enter your configuration when prompted:  <br/>   * API key  <br/>   * Host URL (if using custom endpoint)  <br/>   * Organization ID (if using organization tracking)  <br/>   * Project identifier (if using project management)<br/><br/>Enterprise Deployment<br/><br/>For enterprise deployments, you can pre-configure these values using environment variables or configuration files to ensure consistent governance across your organization.<br/><br/>## Using Goose for Free​<br/><br/>Goose is a free and open source AI agent that you can start using right away, but not all supported LLM Providers provide a free tier.<br/><br/>Below, we outline a couple of free options and how to get started with them.<br/><br/>Limitations<br/><br/>These free options are a great way to get started with Goose and explore its capabilities. However, you may need to upgrade your LLM for better performance.<br/><br/>### Google Gemini​<br/><br/>Google Gemini provides a free tier. To start using the Gemini API with Goose, you need an API Key from Google AI studio.<br/><br/>To set up Google Gemini with Goose, follow these steps:<br/><br/>* Goose Desktop<br/>* Goose CLI<br/><br/>**To update your LLM provider and API key:**<br/><br/>1. Click on the three dots in the top-right corner.<br/>2. Select `Provider Settings` from the menu.<br/>3. Choose `Google Gemini` as provider from the list.<br/>4. Click Edit, enter your API key, and click `Set as Active`.<br/><br/>1. Run:<br/><br/>```<br/>goose configure<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Select `Configure Providers` from the menu.<br/>2. Follow the prompts to choose `Google Gemini` as the provider.<br/>3. Enter your API key when prompted.<br/>4. Enter the Gemini model of your choice.<br/><br/>```<br/>┌   goose-configure<br/>│<br/>◇ What would you like to configure?<br/>│ Configure Providers<br/>│<br/>◇ Which model provider should we use?<br/>│ Google Gemini<br/>│<br/>◇ Provider Google Gemini requires GOOGLE_API_KEY, please enter a value<br/>│▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪<br/>│    <br/>◇ Enter a model from that provider:<br/>│ gemini-2.0-flash-exp<br/>│<br/>◇ Hello! You're all set and ready to go, feel free to ask me anything!<br/>│<br/>└ Configuration saved successfully<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>### Local LLMs​<br/><br/>Ollama and Ramalama are both options to provide local LLMs, each which requires a bit more set up before you can use one of them with Goose.<br/><br/>#### Ollama​<br/><br/>1. Download Ollama.<br/>2. Run any model supporting tool-calling:<br/><br/>Limited Support for models without tool calling<br/><br/>Goose extensively uses tool calling, so models without it (e.g. `DeepSeek-r1`) can only do chat completion. If using models without tool calling, all Goose extensions must be disabled. As an alternative, you can use a custom DeepSeek-r1 model we've made specifically for Goose.<br/><br/>Example:<br/><br/>```<br/>ollama run qwen2.5<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. In a separate terminal window, configure with Goose:<br/><br/>```<br/>goose configure<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Choose to `Configure Providers`<br/><br/>```<br/>┌   goose-configure <br/>│<br/>◆  What would you like to configure?<br/>│  ● Configure Providers (Change provider or update credentials)<br/>│  ○ Toggle Extensions <br/>│  ○ Add Extension <br/>└  <br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Choose `Ollama` as the model provider<br/><br/>```<br/>┌   goose-configure <br/>│<br/>◇  What would you like to configure?<br/>│  Configure Providers <br/>│<br/>◆  Which model provider should we use?<br/>│  ○ Anthropic <br/>│  ○ Databricks <br/>│  ○ Google Gemini <br/>│  ○ Groq <br/>│  ● Ollama (Local open source models)<br/>│  ○ OpenAI <br/>│  ○ OpenRouter <br/>└  <br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Enter the host where your model is running<br/><br/>Endpoint<br/><br/>For Ollama, if you don't provide a host, we set it to `localhost:11434`. When constructing the URL, we prepend `http://` if the scheme is not `http` or `https`. If you're running Ollama on a different server, you'll have to set `OLLAMA_HOST=http://\{host\}:\{port\}`.<br/><br/>```<br/>┌   goose-configure <br/>│<br/>◇  What would you like to configure?<br/>│  Configure Providers <br/>│<br/>◇  Which model provider should we use?<br/>│  Ollama <br/>│<br/>◆  Provider Ollama requires OLLAMA_HOST, please enter a value<br/>│  http://localhost:11434<br/>└<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Enter the model you have running<br/><br/>```<br/>┌   goose-configure <br/>│<br/>◇  What would you like to configure?<br/>│  Configure Providers <br/>│<br/>◇  Which model provider should we use?<br/>│  Ollama <br/>│<br/>◇  Provider Ollama requires OLLAMA_HOST, please enter a value<br/>│  http://localhost:11434<br/>│<br/>◇  Enter a model from that provider:<br/>│  qwen2.5<br/>│<br/>◇  Welcome! You're all set to explore and utilize my capabilities. Let's get started on solving your problems together!<br/>│<br/>└  Configuration saved successfully<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>#### Ramalama​<br/><br/>1. Download Ramalama.<br/>2. Run any Ollama model supporting tool-calling or GGUF format HuggingFace Model :<br/><br/>Limited Support for models without tool calling<br/><br/>Goose extensively uses tool calling, so models without it (e.g. `DeepSeek-r1`) can only do chat completion. If using models without tool calling, all Goose extensions must be disabled. As an alternative, you can use a custom DeepSeek-r1 model we've made specifically for Goose.<br/><br/>Example:<br/><br/>```<br/># NOTE: the --runtime-args="--jinja" flag is required for Ramalama to work with the Goose Ollama provider.<br/>ramalama serve --runtime-args="--jinja" ollama://qwen2.5<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. In a separate terminal window, configure with Goose:<br/><br/>```<br/>goose configure<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Choose to `Configure Providers`<br/><br/>```<br/>┌   goose-configure<br/>│<br/>◆  What would you like to configure?<br/>│  ● Configure Providers (Change provider or update credentials)<br/>│  ○ Toggle Extensions<br/>│  ○ Add Extension<br/>└<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Choose `Ollama` as the model provider since Ramalama is API compatible and can use the Goose Ollama provider<br/><br/>```<br/>┌   goose-configure<br/>│<br/>◇  What would you like to configure?<br/>│  Configure Providers<br/>│<br/>◆  Which model provider should we use?<br/>│  ○ Anthropic<br/>│  ○ Databricks<br/>│  ○ Google Gemini<br/>│  ○ Groq<br/>│  ● Ollama (Local open source models)<br/>│  ○ OpenAI<br/>│  ○ OpenRouter<br/>└<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Enter the host where your model is running<br/><br/>Endpoint<br/><br/>For the Ollama provider, if you don't provide a host, we set it to `localhost:11434`. When constructing the URL, we preprend `http://` if the scheme is not `http` or `https`. Since Ramalama's default port to serve on is 8080, we set `OLLAMA_HOST=http://0.0.0.0:8080`<br/><br/>```<br/>┌   goose-configure<br/>│<br/>◇  What would you like to configure?<br/>│  Configure Providers<br/>│<br/>◇  Which model provider should we use?<br/>│  Ollama<br/>│<br/>◆  Provider Ollama requires OLLAMA_HOST, please enter a value<br/>│  http://0.0.0.0:8080<br/>└<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Enter the model you have running<br/><br/>```<br/>┌   goose-configure<br/>│<br/>◇  What would you like to configure?<br/>│  Configure Providers<br/>│<br/>◇  Which model provider should we use?<br/>│  Ollama<br/>│<br/>◇  Provider Ollama requires OLLAMA_HOST, please enter a value<br/>│  http://0.0.0.0:8080<br/>│<br/>◇  Enter a model from that provider:<br/>│  qwen2.5<br/>│<br/>◇  Welcome! You're all set to explore and utilize my capabilities. Let's get started on solving your problems together!<br/>│<br/>└  Configuration saved successfully<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>### DeepSeek-R1​<br/><br/>Ollama provides open source LLMs, such as `DeepSeek-r1`, that you can install and run locally. Note that the native `DeepSeek-r1` model doesn't support tool calling, however, we have a custom model you can use with Goose.<br/><br/>warning<br/><br/>Note that this is a 70B model size and requires a powerful device to run smoothly.<br/><br/>1. Download and install Ollama from ollama.com.<br/>2. In a terminal window, run the following command to install the custom DeepSeek-r1 model:<br/><br/>```<br/>ollama run michaelneale/deepseek-r1-goose<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>* Goose Desktop<br/>* Goose CLI<br/><br/>1. Click `...` in the top-right corner.<br/>2. Navigate to `Advanced Settings` \-> `Browse Models` \-> and select `Ollama` from the list.<br/>3. Enter `michaelneale/deepseek-r1-goose` for the model name.<br/><br/>1. In a separate terminal window, configure with Goose:<br/><br/>```<br/>goose configure<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Choose to `Configure Providers`<br/><br/>```<br/>┌   goose-configure <br/>│<br/>◆  What would you like to configure?<br/>│  ● Configure Providers (Change provider or update credentials)<br/>│  ○ Toggle Extensions <br/>│  ○ Add Extension <br/>└  <br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Choose `Ollama` as the model provider<br/><br/>```<br/>┌   goose-configure <br/>│<br/>◇  What would you like to configure?<br/>│  Configure Providers <br/>│<br/>◆  Which model provider should we use?<br/>│  ○ Anthropic <br/>│  ○ Databricks <br/>│  ○ Google Gemini <br/>│  ○ Groq <br/>│  ● Ollama (Local open source models)<br/>│  ○ OpenAI <br/>│  ○ OpenRouter <br/>└  <br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Enter the host where your model is running<br/><br/>```<br/>┌   goose-configure <br/>│<br/>◇  What would you like to configure?<br/>│  Configure Providers <br/>│<br/>◇  Which model provider should we use?<br/>│  Ollama <br/>│<br/>◆  Provider Ollama requires OLLAMA_HOST, please enter a value<br/>│  http://localhost:11434<br/>└<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Enter the installed model from above<br/><br/>```<br/>┌   goose-configure <br/>│<br/>◇  What would you like to configure?<br/>│  Configure Providers <br/>│<br/>◇  Which model provider should we use?<br/>│  Ollama <br/>│<br/>◇   Provider Ollama requires OLLAMA_HOST, please enter a value<br/>│  http://localhost:11434  <br/>│    <br/>◇  Enter a model from that provider:<br/>│  michaelneale/deepseek-r1-goose<br/>│<br/>◇  Welcome! You're all set to explore and utilize my capabilities. Let's get started on solving your problems together!<br/>│<br/>└  Configuration saved successfully<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>## Azure OpenAI Credential Chain​<br/><br/>Goose supports two authentication methods for Azure OpenAI:<br/><br/>1. **API Key Authentication** \- Uses the `AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY` for direct authentication<br/>2. **Azure Credential Chain** \- Uses Azure CLI credentials automatically without requiring an API key<br/><br/>To use the Azure Credential Chain:<br/><br/>* Ensure you're logged in with `az login`<br/>* Have appropriate Azure role assignments for the Azure OpenAI service<br/>* Configure with `goose configure` and select Azure OpenAI, leaving the API key field empty<br/><br/>This method simplifies authentication and enhances security for enterprise environments.<br/><br/>---<br/><br/>If you have any questions or need help with a specific provider, feel free to reach out to us on Discord or on the Goose repo.<br/><br/>PreviousInstall GooseNextUsing Extensions<br/><br/>* Available Providers<br/>* CLI Providers<br/>* Configure Provider<br/>* Using Custom OpenAI Endpoints  <br/>   * Configuration Parameters  <br/>   * Example Configurations  <br/>   * Setup Instructions<br/>* Using Goose for Free  <br/>   * Google Gemini  <br/>   * Local LLMs  <br/>   * DeepSeek-R1<br/>* Azure OpenAI Credential Chain<br/><br/>Quick Links<br/><br/>* Install Goose<br/>* Extensions<br/><br/>Community<br/><br/>* Spotlight<br/>* Discord<br/>* YouTube<br/>* LinkedIn<br/>* Twitter / X<br/>* BlueSky<br/>* Nostr<br/><br/>More<br/><br/>* Blog<br/>* GitHub<br/><br/>Copyright © 2025 Block, Inc. |

What the web docs actually say (no hand-waving)

1. Goose has a “CLI provider” named **claude-code** (docs: *Configure LLM Provider → CLI Providers*).  
   – It simply shells out to the Claude CLI you already installed.  
   – So every normal `goose …` command can run on Claude Code’s 200 k-token model if you set  
     `GOOSE_PROVIDER=claude-code`.

2. There is **no built-in “github-index” recipe or sub-command** in Goose.  
   – The recipes directory contains only demos; anything else you must write yourself.  
   – Therefore the error: *unrecognized subcommand 'github-index'*.

3. Goose’s recommended way to feed a repo to Claude is with the loader syntax:

```
goose --loader dir=/path/to/repo \
      --model claude-code \
      --format json \
      -- \
"Produce a JSON system-map of this repository:
 - list top-level packages/services
 - enumerate enums/constants
 - detect REST/API routes
 - count unit tests
Return ONLY valid JSON."
```

• `--loader dir=` streams the entire file tree to Claude Code.  
• `--format json` tells Goose to insist on valid JSON in the reply.  
• Everything after `--` is the prompt.

How we’ll use that in the ingestion worker

```bash
export GOOSE_PROVIDER=claude-code      # once at startup
export CLAUDE_TOKEN=…                  # whatever the CLI expects

# inside ingestionWorker.js
const gooseArgs = [
  '--loader', `dir=${workDir}`,
  '--model',  'claude-code',
  '--format', 'json',
  '--',
  PROMPT_TEXT
]
await run('goose', gooseArgs)
```

If the command exits 0 and the stdout parses as JSON, we write it to
`system-map.json`, emit `project.indexed`, and the UI turns green.
Nothing to “recipe” or “subcommand”—just one prompt.

Next change (what I’ll implement if you approve)

1. Remove the `github-index` call from `ingestionWorker.js`.  
2. Drop in the loader-prompt call shown above.  
3. Add a timeout (e.g. 120 s) so a huge repo doesn’t hang forever.  
4. Log Goose’s stderr so we can see if Claude says it hit a token limit.

After that the worker will successfully generate a system map using Claude Code—exactly as the docs prescribe—no hallucination involved.

Development<br/><br/># Resolving CI Issues with Goose: A Practical Walkthrough<br/><br/>December 11, 2024 · 4 min read<br/><br/>Dalton Turner<br/><br/>Dalton Turner<br/><br/>Software Engineer<br/><br/>CI<br/><br/>Running into Continuous Integration (CI) failures in pull requests can be quite frustrating but they happen very often. In this post, we leverage the GitHub CLI (`gh`) using Goose to simplify your CI debugging process, fetch detailed information about failed CI runs and annotations directly from GitHub, and even apply fixes directly.<br/><br/>Goose Beta Version<br/><br/>This post was written about a beta version of Goose and the commands and flow may have changed.<br/><br/>## Getting Started​<br/><br/>Before diving in, ensure you have the necessary tools set up.<br/><br/>### 1\. Install and Authenticate GitHub CLI (`gh`)​<br/><br/>You'll need the GitHub CLI `gh` to enable Goose's access to CI check run details.<br/><br/>```<br/>brew install gh<br/>gh auth login<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>Follow the prompts to authenticate your account.<br/><br/>### 2\. Configure Goose​<br/><br/>Ensure Goose is configured and ready to interact with your repository and local tools. Specifically, you will need to configure a goose profile with the GitHub toolkit.<br/><br/>Update your `profiles.yaml` file in `~/.config/goose` with the necessary toolkits:<br/><br/>```<br/>my-profile:<br/>  provider: anthropic<br/>  processor: claude-3-5-sonnet<br/>  accelerator: claude-3-5-sonnet<br/>  moderator: truncate<br/>  toolkits:<br/>    - name: developer<br/>      requires: \{}<br/>    - name: github<br/>      requires: \{}<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>Start a session with the profile:<br/><br/>```<br/>goose session start --profile my-profile<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>If the profile’s toolkits are not correctly configured, Goose might fail to access `gh` commands.<br/><br/>## Resolving CI Failures with Goose​<br/><br/>Once everything is set up, we can now use Goose to tackle CI issues with the following steps:<br/><br/>### Step 1: Fetch CI Failure Details​<br/><br/>Ask Goose to retrieve information about the CI failures for a specific PR.<br/><br/>**Example Request:**<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>Can you tell me about the CI failures on PR #11111 in the organization/repo repository? The check run ID is 123456.<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>You can access a check run ID by clicking on a PR’s checks tab and selecting a failure. The ID will be available in the URL.<br/><br/>**Goose's Workflow:**<br/><br/>Goose will use the `gh` CLI to check run information and provide a detailed summary of the issues. Goose uses the GitHub CLI to:<br/><br/>* Fetch details about failed CI runs, including logs and annotations.<br/>* Provide a clear and actionable summary of issues.<br/><br/>**Example Command Goose Runs:**<br/><br/>```<br/>gh api -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" /repos/<owner>/<repo>/check-runs/<check-run-id>/annotations<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>**Example Goose Output:**<br/><br/>```<br/>Here are the details for Check Run ID 123456:<br/><br/>**Name**: CI-Build-All  <br/>**Status**: completed  <br/>**Conclusion**: failure  <br/><br/>**Annotations Summary:**  <br/>1. **ModuleA Test Failure**  <br/>   File: `ModuleATests`  <br/>   Line: 35  <br/>   Error: Mismatched parameter order in function call.  <br/><br/>2. **ModuleB Test Failure**  <br/>   File: `ModuleBTests`  <br/>   Line: 64  <br/>   Error: Unexpected nil value encountered during initialization.  <br/><br/>3. **ModuleC Test Failure**  <br/>   File: `ModuleCTests`  <br/>   Line: 98  <br/>   Error: Type mismatch in returned value. Expected 'String', found 'Int'.  <br/><br/>```<br/><br/>### Step 2: Request Fixes from Goose​<br/><br/>Once Goose provides the failure details, ask it to resolve the issues directly.<br/><br/>Example Request:<br/><br/>```<br/>Can you fix these issues and stage the changes so I can review them? Do not add unnecessary code comments.<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>**What Goose Does:**<br/><br/>* Applies fixes based on error messages.<br/>* Stages changes for review.<br/><br/>**Example Goose Response:**<br/><br/>```<br/>I have fixed the following files and staged them:<br/><br/>- `ModuleATests`: Corrected the order of parameters in the function call.  <br/>- `ModuleBTests`: Resolved the unexpected nil value encountered during initialization.  <br/>- `ModuleCTests`: Adjusted the type mismatch in the returned value.  <br/><br/>You can now review the staged changes.<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>### Step 3: Review the Changes​<br/><br/>Carefully review the staged changes to ensure they address the issues correctly and avoid unintended modifications.<br/><br/>**Things to Check:**<br/><br/>* No unnecessary comments (e.g., // Fix xyz).<br/>* No alterations to unrelated parts of the code.<br/><br/>If needed, clean up or re-stage the changes before committing.<br/><br/>## Benefits of Using Goose​<br/><br/>Using Goose to resolve CI issues streamlines your workflow by:<br/><br/>* identifying issues and applying fixes with minimal manual effort.<br/>* integrating with tools like the GitHub CLI to validate changes.<br/>* handling repetitive CI debugging tasks while you focus on code quality.<br/><br/>Goose allows you to resolve CI failures efficiently, ensuring confidence in your workflow while reducing the effort required for debugging and testing.<br/><br/>Try it out, and let Goose handle the heavy lifting of CI debugging for you!<br/><br/>Newer postIntroducing codename gooseOlder postConnecting AI Agents to Your Systems with MCP<br/><br/>* Getting Started  <br/>   * 1\. Install and Authenticate GitHub CLI (gh)  <br/>   * 2\. Glossary<br/>4. **1.** Getting Started<br/>5. 1. **1.1.** Creating A Load test  <br/>   2. **1.2.** Validating Requests  <br/>   3. **1.3.** Running A Load Test  <br/>   4. **1.4.** Run-Time Options  <br/>   5. 1. **1.4.1.** Common Options  <br/>         2. **1.4.2.** Test Plan  <br/>         3. **1.4.3.** Throttle  <br/>         4. **1.4.4.** Limiting Scenarios  <br/>         5. **1.4.5.** Custom Options  <br/>   6. **1.5.** Metrics  <br/>   7. **1.6.** Tips<br/>6. **2.** Logging<br/>7. 1. **2.1.** Request Log  <br/>   2. **2.2.** Transaction Log  <br/>   3. **2.3.** Scenario Log  <br/>   4. **2.4.** Error Log  <br/>   5. **2.5.** Debug Log<br/>8. **3.** Controllers<br/>9. 1. **3.1.** Telnet Controller  <br/>   2. **3.2.** WebSocket Controller<br/>10. **4.** Gaggle: Distributed Load Test<br/>11. 1. **4.1.** Manager  <br/>   2. **4.2.** Worker  <br/>   3. **4.3.** Configuration  <br/>   4. **4.4.** Technical details<br/>12. **5.** Coordinated Omission<br/>13. 1. **5.1.** Mitigation  <br/>   2. **5.2.** Metrics<br/>14. **6.** Configuration<br/>15. 1. **6.1.** Defaults  <br/>   2. **6.2.** Scheduling Scenarios And Transactions  <br/>   3. **6.3.** RustLS<br/>16. **7.** Examples<br/>17. 1. **7.1.** Simple  <br/>   2. **7.2.** Closure  <br/>   3. **7.3.** Session  <br/>   4. **7.4.** Drupal Memcache  <br/>   5. **7.5.** Umami<br/><br/>* Light<br/>* Rust<br/>* Coal<br/>* Navy<br/>* Ayu<br/><br/># The Goose Book<br/><br/># Transaction Log<br/><br/>Goose can optionally log details about each time a transaction is run during a load test. To enable, add the `--transaction-log <transaction.log>` command line option, where `<transaction.log>` is either a relative or absolute path of the log file to create. Any existing file that may already exist will be overwritten.<br/><br/>Logs include the entire TransactionMetric object which is created each time any transaction is run.<br/><br/>## Log Format<br/><br/>By default, logs are written in JSON Lines format. For example:<br/><br/>```json<br/>\{"elapsed":22060,"name":"(Anon) front page","run_time":97,"success":true,"transaction_index":0,"scenario_index":0,"user":0\}<br/>\{"elapsed":22118,"name":"(Anon) node page","run_time":41,"success":true,"transaction_index":1,"scenario_index":0,"user":5\}<br/>\{"elapsed":22157,"name":"(Anon) node page","run_time":6,"success":true,"transaction_index":1,"scenario_index":0,"user":0\}<br/>\{"elapsed":22078,"name":"(Auth) front page","run_time":109,"success":true,"transaction_index":1,"scenario_index":1,"user":6\}<br/>\{"elapsed":22157,"name":"(Anon) user page","run_time":35,"success":true,"transaction_index":2,"scenario_index":0,"user":4\}<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>In the first line of the above example, `GooseUser` thread 0 succesfully ran the `(Anon) front page` transaction in 97 milliseconds. In the second line `GooseUser` thread 5 succesfully ran the `(Anon) node page` transaction in 41 milliseconds.<br/><br/>The `--transaction-format` option can be used to log in `csv`, `json` (default), `raw` or `pretty` format. The `raw` format is Rust's debug output of the entire TransactionMetric object.<br/><br/>For example, `csv` output of similar transactions as those logged above would like like:<br/><br/>```csv<br/>elapsed,scenario_index,transaction_index,name,run_time,success,user<br/>21936,0,0,"(Anon) front page",83,true,0<br/>21990,1,3,"(Auth) user page",34,true,1<br/>21954,0,0,"(Anon) front page",84,true,5<br/>22009,0,1,"(Anon) node page",34,true,2<br/>21952,0,0,"(Anon) front page",95,true,7<br/><br/>```<br/><br/># Gaggle Mode<br/><br/>When operating in Gaggle-mode, the `--transaction-log` option can only be enabled on the Worker processes, configuring Goose to spread out the overhead of writing logs. |

                                 \|                     \|                  \|<br/><br/>## Repository files navigation<br/><br/>* README<br/>* Code of conduct<br/>* MIT license<br/><br/># Goose<br/><br/>Wanna run jenkins in your cli? Use goose!<br/><br/>To install<br/><br/>```<br/> cd goose<br/> go install .<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>(go needs to be previously installed on your system)<br/><br/>## Command Summary<br/><br/>### run<br/><br/>Goose run will invoke a jenkins job based on the current git directory and branch. If you want to pick a job manually, specify the path of the job. Running goose with the syntax below assumes your go binaries path is on your system path. If not, you can replace 'goose' with 'go run .' from your goose directory.<br/><br/>```<br/>goose run # Will list available jobs based on your directory<br/><br/>goose run Example/Folder/CreateThing/mainbranch # Run the CreateThing job on the mainbranch branch.<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>### jobs<br/><br/>Print out the list of jobs in a jenkins directory. (Root directory by default)<br/><br/>```<br/>❯ goose jobs<br/>Example<br/>Example2<br/>...<br/><br/>❯ goose jobs Example<br/>SubJob1<br/>SubJob2<br/><br/><br/>```<br/><br/>### Latest<br/><br/>Latest will print out the output of the latest running job of the given job OR based on the current git/branch.<br/><br/>### Search<br/><br/>Search will list out the jenkins jobs relevant to your current git directory<br/><br/>### RunList<br/><br/>Runlist will run jobs concurrently from a batchfile. For example:<br/><br/>```<br/>cat <<EOF >>myBatchFile<br/>BatchJobs:<br/>  - Job: Path/To/My/Job<br/>    Variables:<br/>      VariableA: True<br/>      VariableB: False<br/>    Substitute:<br/>      VariableC: [value1,value2]<br/>EOF<br/><br/>goose runlist myBatchFile<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>Will run 2 jobs concurrently for the `Path/To/My/Job` on the main branch. The `VariableA` and `VariableB` variables will be the same for these 4 job runs. The end result is that each job is run with the same variables with `VariableC` being different for each run.<br/><br/>## Requirements<br/><br/>You'll need to define JENKINS\_EMAIL and JENKINS\_API\_KEY and JENKINS\_ROOT and JENKINS\_LOGIN\_URL. The api key needs to be made at JENKINS\_ROOT/me/configure.<br/><br/>If you're using an enterprise jenkins setup, double check that you can reach all jobs from the root URL. Your JENKINS\_ROOT should have no path (i.e, <https://ci.mycompany.com>). Your JENKINS\_LOGIN\_URL contains the path to the root job directory (i.e, <https://ci.mycompany.com/path/job/Base>).<br/><br/>If you are using an enterprise Jenkins setup, the login url is most likely similar to <https://ci.mycompany.com/cjob/job/BaseFolderName><br/><br/>## About<br/><br/> CLI interface for Jenkins<br/><br/>### Resources<br/><br/> Readme <br/><br/>### License<br/><br/> MIT license <br/><br/>### Code of conduct<br/><br/> Code of conduct <br/><br/>###  Uh oh!<br/><br/>There was an error while loading. Repository files navigation<br/><br/>* README<br/>* Code of conduct<br/>* MIT license<br/>* Security<br/><br/># Goose, the git ops service.<br/><br/>Build Status Known Vulnerabilities CII Best Practices<br/><br/>Goose is a tool which simplifies gitops by mapping between "files/file patterns I care about" and "services that need to know about those changes".<br/><br/>* Known Limitations<br/>* Why?<br/>* How to use it<br/>* How to configure it<br/>* Backing service API contract<br/>* FAQ<br/><br/>## Known limitations currently<br/><br/>> ⚠ This repository is not "done" and is shared in the spirit of developing in the open. Provide feedback & get involved so we can shape this into something awesome.<br/><br/>Big things you probably care about:<br/><br/>1. There is no auth mechanism between goose & the backing services.<br/>2. The auth mechanism ^^ should ideally be pluggable to handle your systems' special auth requirements.<br/>3. Support for regex matching<br/>4. No way to limit which repositories a given hook runs for. It's either everyone or no one.<br/><br/>## Why?<br/><br/>We have found examples of services which require us to configure resources by clicking around UIs. This suffers from an inability to review the work that's done before it happens, making rollbacks more difficult and an inability to add automated tooling around it. GitOpssolves this.<br/><br/>There are some natural struggles for adopting a gitops-oriented approach. First, services who want to offer gitops functionality would need to listen to repository webhooks (which are a bit of a pain to setup, especially for every repository). They'd also need to build functionality around checking out git repositories, which significantly changes the scope of their existing APIs.<br/><br/>To provide an easier experience for both application developers and framework teams, we're building an intermediary layer between the hooks that GitHub provides and the services which want to know about the changes.<br/><br/>The end goal is you simply:<br/><br/>1. Add our webhook & github user to your org<br/>2. Check in the relevant files<br/>3. Profit!<br/><br/>The service sends events for both `VERIFY` actions, like when a pull request is created, as well as `COMMIT` actions, which are when the change actually needs to take place. For `VERIFY` actions, these will be represented in the PR status.<br/><br/>## How?<br/><br/>To get started, we need github credentials and a config file to tell goose what it should do.<br/><br/>GitHub credentials can be either specified from environment variables (`GITHUB_USERNAME`, `GITHUB_PASSWORD`), or goose will look in the contents of`/etc/secrets/GITHUB_USERNAME` and `/etc/secrets/GITHUB_PASSWORD` for use with kubernetes-oriented volume mounts.<br/><br/>Goose is built to run inside a docker container (or kubernetes pod), so it uses Dockerfiles for setup & running. To pass in a config file, goose looks at the `GOOSE_CONFIG` environment variable for a file location, defaulting to `/etc/goose.yml`.<br/><br/>A simple, example Dockerfile might look like:<br/><br/>FROM docker.io/ebay/goose:latest<br/>COPY path/to/my/config.yml /etc/goose.yml<br/>ENV GOOSE_CONFIG /etc/goose.yml # technically redundant since this is the default.<br/>ENV GITHUB_USERNAME myusername<br/>ENV GITHUB_PASSWORD very-secret<br/><br/>You can deploy that Dockerfile with your hosting provider and get honkin'.<br/><br/>For local setup instructions, check out the contributing guide<br/><br/>## Config File<br/><br/>The config file holds the mapping of the filenames/globs you care about alongside the url you wish us to call. It also holds information so we can track down who a particular endpoint belongs to.<br/><br/>Example:<br/><br/>```<br/>- name: Alarm creation<br/>  owner: vjay<br/>  filePattern: alarms.yaml<br/>  url: my-alarm-service.example.org/create-from-yaml<br/><br/>- name: Creation of group permissions<br/>  owner: jabrahms<br/>  filePattern: **/*/OWNERS.(json\|yaml)<br/>  includeOld: true<br/>  url: identity-control.example.org/<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>When one of our repositories updates their `alarms.yaml` file, goose will fetch the newest version of that file sent to the relevant url.<br/><br/>In the group permissions, goose sends over the old file (e.g. before the change was made) in addition to the new one, if any `OWNERS.yaml` or `OWNERS.json`files match in any folder.<br/><br/>This is the format of the config in this repository to get the functionality to work.<br/><br/>```<br/>name: A human-readable name for what the service does<br/>owner: Contact information so we can track down the relevant owners.<br/>url: The URL that will receive the request for processing the event.<br/>filePatterns: (list of strings) files you're hoping to find. This supports both exact matches as well as glob patterns (including globstar support)<br/>includeOld: boolean, default=false. Whether to send the previous version's file contents<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>## Service Provider API<br/><br/>This is the data format we send to the upstream systems.<br/><br/>```<br/>appId: name of app according to infohub<br/>eventTimestamp: when the event source happened<br/>source: Object<br/>  uri: a URI to the resource in question<br/>  sha: the commit id for this change for use as a unique identifier<br/>type: enum of either VERIFY or COMMIT. Verify is for pre-flight checks like pull request validations<br/>files: []File<br/><br/>File:<br/>  filepath: full path to the file, relative to the repository root<br/>  matchType: enum of EXACT_MATCH or GLOB_M`ATCH<br/>  contents:<br/>    new: (optional) string of file contents after change<br/>    old: (optional) string of file contents before change<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>### Example<br/><br/>\{<br/>    "appId": "jabrahms_goose",<br/>    "eventTimestamp": "2021-12-28T11:14:37Z",<br/>    "source": \{<br/>        "uri": "https://github-enterprise.example.com/...",<br/>        "sha": "039282900a938e020c08320"<br/>    \},<br/>    "type": "VERIFY",<br/>    "files": [\{<br/>        "filepath": "alarms.yaml",<br/>        "matchType": "EXACT_MATCH",<br/>        "contents": \{<br/>            "new": "...contents here..."<br/>        \}<br/>    \}]<br/>\}<br/><br/># FAQ<br/><br/>## Why goose?<br/><br/>It stands for GitOpsSErvice (or git oops service, if you prefer).<br/><br/>## Does this help me get slack notifications or something?<br/><br/>Sorta! This really serves as an intermediate layer between git and the systems you may have internally to accomplish such things. Goose needs a webservice on the other side to talk with. The value proposition to those web services is that they don't have to learn what a git repository is or convince developers to setup yet another git hook.<br/><br/>So your alarms system team would integrate with goose. They would define a file format that you should write and the file names that they'll pay attention to. When you make those changes, goose will connect your commits with their service.<br/><br/>## About<br/><br/> A robot for mapping github events into actionable HTTP payloads<br/><br/>### Topics<br/><br/> github  devops  gitops <br/><br/>### Resources<br/><br/> Readme <br/><br/>### License<br/><br/> MIT license <br/><br/>### Code of conduct<br/><br/> Code of conduct <br/><br/>### Security policy<br/><br/> Security policy <br/><br/>###  Uh oh!<br/><br/>There was an error while loading.
