go.spiff.io/jsondir<br/><br/>jsondir is a tool to map directory structures and their contents to JSON.<br/><br/>It walks a directory tree and convert files found to what it thinks is an<br/>appropriate JSON representation. Boolean values are true/TRUE and false/FALSE,<br/>numerics are any normal value handled by strconv.ParseInt, floats any string<br/>convertible by strconv.ParseFloat, the string "null" or "NULL" is a null value,<br/>and everything else is treated as a string. Type precedence is null, boolean,<br/>integer, float, and then string as a catch-all. Empty files are empty strings,<br/>and jsondir will by default trim trailing spaces.<br/><br/>Files ending in an '@' (at sign) are treated as raw JSON values and will be<br/>unmarshaled upon loading to verify they're valid. Invalid data is a failure.<br/>Each tree walked is emitted as a separate JSON blob, with each blob separated by<br/>a newline. If the output is not compact, there is still a newline separating the<br/>start and end of the JSON blobs.<br/><br/>If the -x flag is set, executable files will be run to generate JSON output.<br/>This can be used to nest jsondir calls if necessary (e.g., including a separate<br/>directory tree). By default, executable files are run in a temporary directory,<br/>just for the sake of confusing them. You can disable this by passing -rx or -nt<br/>to either execute files in the directory they're located in or in jsondir's<br/>working directory, respectively.<br/><br/>By default, dot files are ignored. If you pass an ignore parameter, this default<br/>no longer applies.<br/><br/>Each path is converted to a JSON value. The path may refer to a file or<br/>directory -- in the case of a directory, it will produce either an object or an<br/>array. If a directory's name ends in "[]" (minus quotes), the directory is<br/>treated as an array. If the name ends in "\{}", it's an object. The first of<br/>either "\{}" or "[]" are trimmed from key names when nesting directories. As<br/>such, to include "[]" at the end of a directory's key name without turning the<br/>directory into an array, you can name it "yourDirectory[]\{}".<br/><br/><br/>Usage<br/>-----<br/><br/>   jsondir [OPTIONS] [path...]<br/><br/><br/>Options<br/>-------<br/><br/>All boolean flags can be passed as their name only to imply true. E.g., -v is<br/>the same as -v=true. All boolean flags default to false except for -c (compact).<br/><br/>-v=true\|false<br/>   Enable verbose logging. Useful for debugging, not much else.<br/><br/>-c=true\|false<br/>   Emit compact output. This defaults to false if stdout is a TTY.<br/><br/>-s=true\|false<br/>   Whether to follow symlinks. By default, symlinks are ignored.<br/><br/>-ws=true\|false<br/>   Whether to keep trailing whitespace.<br/><br/>-x=true\|false<br/>   Run executables to produce output. Off by default for obvious sanity reasons.<br/><br/>-nt=true\|false<br/>   If -x is true, -nt tells jsondir to run executables from the PWD instead of<br/>   a temporary directory. If your executables are safe and well-behaved, this is<br/>   probably fine.<br/><br/>-rx=true\|false<br/>   If -x is true, -rx tells jsondir to run executables from the executables'<br/>   directory instead of the PWD. navigation<br/><br/>* README<br/>* MIT license<br/><br/># GIEx1<br/><br/>A new, unique injection method via replacing `updater` require path (Windows only).<br/><br/>## Method<br/><br/>GIEx1 relies on Discord's new updater API (referred to as v2 in this document). v2 uses a native Rust library which the client (code within `app.asar`) `require`'s. By replacing this, you can get code execution within the `app.asar`. What this project does:<br/><br/>* Make a directory with the original name (`updater`)<br/>* Move the original native library within (`updater.node` moves into the `updater` dir)<br/>* Make an `index.js` file with our custom code, which:  <br/>   * Makes a class extending the native library's  <br/>   * Hooks into functions to:  <br/>         * Forcing update endpoint to have mods (GooseMod as an example) injected  <br/>         * Rehook GIEx1 into any new updates<br/><br/>## Install<br/><br/>Installation is similar to the info about what the code does above. Simple steps:<br/><br/>1. Download / clone this repo<br/>2. Rename `src` to `updater`<br/>3. Copy your `updater.node` from your Discord install (like for stable, `%localappdata%\Discord\app-1.X.Y\`) into the new `updater` directory<br/>4. Remove the `updater.node` from your Discord install directory<br/>5. Copy your `updater` directory into your Discord install directory<br/>6. Restart Discord via system tray<br/><br/>## About<br/><br/> A new, unique injection method via replacing \`updater\` require path (Windows only).<br/><br/>### Resources<br/><br/> Readme <br/><br/>### License<br/><br/> MIT license <br/><br/>###  Uh oh!<br/><br/>There was an error while loading. successfully<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>## Using Custom OpenAI Endpoints​<br/><br/>Goose supports using custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints, which is particularly useful for:<br/><br/>* Self-hosted LLMs (e.g., LLaMA, Mistral) using vLLM or KServe<br/>* Private OpenAI-compatible API servers<br/>* Enterprise deployments requiring data governance and security compliance<br/>* OpenAI API proxies or gateways<br/><br/>### Configuration Parameters​<br/><br/>\| Parameter               \| Required \| Description                                                                                                                                                         \|<br/>\| ----------------------- \| -------- \| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- \|<br/>\| OPENAI\_API\_KEY        \| Yes      \| Authentication key for the API                                                                                                                                      \|<br/>\| OPENAI\_HOST            \| No       \| Custom endpoint URL (defaults to api.openai.com)                                                                                                                    \|<br/>\| OPENAI\_ORGANIZATION    \| No       \| Organization ID for usage tracking and governance                                                                                                                   \|<br/>\| OPENAI\_PROJECT         \| No       \| Project identifier for resource management                                                                                                                          \|<br/>\| OPENAI\_CUSTOM\_HEADERS \| No       \| Additional headers to include in the request. Can be set via environment variable, configuration file, or CLI, in the format HEADER\_A=VALUE\_A,HEADER\_B=VALUE\_B. \|<br/><br/>### Example Configurations​<br/><br/>* vLLM Self-Hosted<br/>* KServe Deployment<br/>* Enterprise OpenAI<br/>* Custom Headers<br/><br/>If you're running LLaMA or other models using vLLM with OpenAI compatibility:<br/><br/>```<br/>OPENAI_HOST=https://your-vllm-endpoint.internal<br/>OPENAI_API_KEY=your-internal-api-key<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>For models deployed on Kubernetes using KServe:<br/><br/>```<br/>OPENAI_HOST=https://kserve-gateway.your-cluster<br/>OPENAI_API_KEY=your-kserve-api-key<br/>OPENAI_ORGANIZATION=your-org-id<br/>OPENAI_PROJECT=ml-serving<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>For enterprise OpenAI deployments with governance:<br/><br/>```<br/>OPENAI_API_KEY=your-api-key<br/>OPENAI_ORGANIZATION=org-id123<br/>OPENAI_PROJECT=compliance-approved<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>For OpenAI-compatible endpoints that require custom headers:<br/><br/>```<br/>OPENAI_API_KEY=your-api-key<br/>OPENAI_ORGANIZATION=org-id123<br/>OPENAI_PROJECT=compliance-approved<br/>OPENAI_CUSTOM_HEADERS="X-Header-A=abc,X-Header-B=def"<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>### Setup Instructions​<br/><br/>* Goose Desktop<br/>* Goose CLI<br/><br/>1. Click `...` in the upper right corner<br/>2. Click `Advanced Settings`<br/>3. Next to `Models`, click the `browse` link<br/>4. Click the `configure` link in the upper right corner<br/>5. Press the `+` button next to OpenAI<br/>6. Fill in your configuration details:  <br/>   * API Key (required)  <br/>   * Host URL (for custom endpoints)  <br/>   * Organization ID (for usage tracking)  <br/>   * Project (for resource management)<br/>7. Press `submit`<br/><br/>1. Run `goose configure`<br/>2. Select `Configure Providers`<br/>3. Choose `OpenAI` as the provider<br/>4. Enter your configuration when prompted:  <br/>   * API key  <br/>   * Host URL (if using custom endpoint)  <br/>   * Organization ID (if using organization tracking)  <br/>   * Project identifier (if using project management)<br/><br/>Enterprise Deployment<br/><br/>For enterprise deployments, you can pre-configure these values using environment variables or configuration files to ensure consistent governance across your organization.<br/><br/>## Using Goose for Free​<br/><br/>Goose is a free and open source AI agent that you can start using right away, but not all supported LLM Providers provide a free tier.<br/><br/>Below, we outline a couple of free options and how to get started with them.<br/><br/>Limitations<br/><br/>These free options are a great way to get started with Goose and explore its capabilities. However, you may need to upgrade your LLM for better performance.<br/><br/>### Google Gemini​<br/><br/>Google Gemini provides a free tier. To start using the Gemini API with Goose, you need an API Key from Google AI studio.<br/><br/>To set up Google Gemini with Goose, follow these steps:<br/><br/>* Goose Desktop<br/>* Goose CLI<br/><br/>**To update your LLM provider and API key:**<br/><br/>1. Click on the three dots in the top-right corner.<br/>2. Select `Provider Settings` from the menu.<br/>3. Choose `Google Gemini` as provider from the list.<br/>4. Click Edit, enter your API key, and click `Set as Active`.<br/><br/>1. Run:<br/><br/>```<br/>goose configure<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Select `Configure Providers` from the menu.<br/>2. Follow the prompts to choose `Google Gemini` as the provider.<br/>3. Enter your API key when prompted.<br/>4. Enter the Gemini model of your choice.<br/><br/>```<br/>┌   goose-configure<br/>│<br/>◇ What would you like to configure?<br/>│ Configure Providers<br/>│<br/>◇ Which model provider should we use?<br/>│ Google Gemini<br/>│<br/>◇ Provider Google Gemini requires GOOGLE_API_KEY, please enter a value<br/>│▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪<br/>│    <br/>◇ Enter a model from that provider:<br/>│ gemini-2.0-flash-exp<br/>│<br/>◇ Hello! You're all set and ready to go, feel free to ask me anything!<br/>│<br/>└ Configuration saved successfully<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>### Local LLMs​<br/><br/>Ollama and Ramalama are both options to provide local LLMs, each which requires a bit more set up before you can use one of them with Goose.<br/><br/>#### Ollama​<br/><br/>1. Download Ollama.<br/>2. Run any model supporting tool-calling:<br/><br/>Limited Support for models without tool calling<br/><br/>Goose extensively uses tool calling, so models without it (e.g. `DeepSeek-r1`) can only do chat completion. If using models without tool calling, all Goose extensions must be disabled. As an alternative, you can use a custom DeepSeek-r1 model we've made specifically for Goose.<br/><br/>Example:<br/><br/>```<br/>ollama run qwen2.5<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. In a separate terminal window, configure with Goose:<br/><br/>```<br/>goose configure<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Choose to `Configure Providers`<br/><br/>```<br/>┌   goose-configure <br/>│<br/>◆  What would you like to configure?<br/>│  ● Configure Providers (Change provider or update credentials)<br/>│  ○ Toggle Extensions <br/>│  ○ Add Extension <br/>└  <br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Choose `Ollama` as the model provider<br/><br/>```<br/>┌   goose-configure <br/>│<br/>◇  What would you like to configure?<br/>│  Configure Providers <br/>│<br/>◆  Which model provider should we use?<br/>│  ○ Anthropic <br/>│  ○ Databricks <br/>│  ○ Google Gemini <br/>│  ○ Groq <br/>│  ● Ollama (Local open source models)<br/>│  ○ OpenAI <br/>│  ○ OpenRouter <br/>└  <br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Enter the host where your model is running<br/><br/>Endpoint<br/><br/>For Ollama, if you don't provide a host, we set it to `localhost:11434`. When constructing the URL, we prepend `http://` if the scheme is not `http` or `https`. If you're running Ollama on a different server, you'll have to set `OLLAMA_HOST=http://\{host\}:\{port\}`.<br/><br/>```<br/>┌   goose-configure <br/>│<br/>◇  What would you like to configure?<br/>│  Configure Providers <br/>│<br/>◇  Which model provider should we use?<br/>│  Ollama <br/>│<br/>◆  Provider Ollama requires OLLAMA_HOST, please enter a value<br/>│  http://localhost:11434<br/>└<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>1. Enter the model you have running<br/><br/>```<br/>┌   goose-configure <br/>│<br/>◇  What would you like to configure?<br/>│  Configure Providers <br/>│<br/>◇  Which model provider should we use?<br/>│  Ollama <br/>│<br/>◇  Provider Ollama requires OLLAMA_HOST, please enter a value<br/>│  http://localhost:11434<br/>│<br/>◇  Enter a model from that provider:<br/>│  qwen2.5<br/>│<br/>◇  Welcome! You're all set to explore and utilize my capabilities. Let's get started on solving your problems together!<br/>│<br/>└  Configuration saved successfully<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>#### Ramalama​<br/><br/>1. Download Ramalama.<br/>2. Development<br/><br/># A Visual Guide To MCP Ecosystem<br/><br/>April 10, 2025 · 4 min read<br/><br/>Ebony Louis<br/><br/>Ebony Louis<br/><br/>Developer Advocate<br/><br/>blog cover<br/><br/>You ever open a GitHub repo or blog post, read the first sentence, and immediately feel like you’ve stumbled into a PhD dissertation?<br/><br/>Yeah. Same.<br/><br/>MCP (Model Context Protocol) sounds complicated, but it’s really not. Think of this as your go to cheat sheet, no whitepapers, no academic jargon, just plain English and a few good visuals.<br/><br/>Let's break this down together.<br/><br/>## What Is MCP in Plain English?​<br/><br/>MCP is like a universal translator between your AI agent, like Goose, and external tools, files, databases, APIs, you name it.<br/><br/>It gives your agent a way to ask questions, run tools, store/retrieve context, and keep track of everything it knows.<br/><br/>Instead of cramming everything into one prompt like “here’s 10k tokens worth of context, good luck,” MCP helps the model pull what it needs, when it needs it.<br/><br/>## Who Are The Players?​<br/><br/>players<br/><br/>* **User** – You, the person with the big ideas and messy problems<br/>* **Agent** – The AI agent, Goose, living in your CLI, IDE, or desktop application<br/>* **LLM** – The model that does the reasoning (like Claude, GPT-4, etc.)<br/>* **MCP Servers (Extensions)** – Goose's toolbox: built-in and custom extensions that give goose the ability to execute tasks<br/><br/>## How Do They Communicate?​<br/><br/>Lets take a look at how all the players work together:<br/><br/>Visual guideIn this flow, the user kicks things off by giving Goose a prompt. Goose gets the prompt ready, along with its available tools and any relevant context, and hands it off to the LLM. The LLM decides which tools it needs to complete the task. Goose then routes those tool calls to the right MCP servers, and they execute the tasks. As steps of the task are being completed, informs you, the user, of what it's done and can also loop with the LLM as needed.<br/><br/>## Here's An Analogy​<br/><br/>Let’s make this even clearer with a James Bond analogy. Sometimes a story makes it all click.<br/><br/>james bond<br/><br/>If you’ve ever seen a James Bond movie, you know the scene, Bond walks into Q’s lab before the mission. Q opens up the suitcase of gadgets, exploding pens, invisible cars, grappling watches, you name it.<br/><br/>Goose is _like_ Q in this situation. The suitcase is already packed with tools, built-in and custom extensions (MCP servers).<br/><br/>Before the LLM (Bond) starts the mission, Goose gives it the full briefing:<br/><br/>> _"Here’s your target (the prompt). Here’s your gadget suitcase (the extensions you can use). Good luck."_<br/><br/>The MCP servers?<br/><br/>That’s the hidden team in the back actually building the gadgets and handing them over when Bond needs them in the field.<br/><br/>The LLM (Bond) picks the right gadgets for the mission, Goose routes the request to the right MCP server, MCP makes sure they work, and the whole operation runs smoothly.<br/><br/>Without Goose handing over the gadget suitcase, the model would just show up in the field with nothing but a tuxedo and a smile, and we don't want to know how that ends.<br/><br/>## Your Turn​<br/><br/>Now that you’ve got the basics down, and you understand how the MCP ecosystem works, it’s time to try it yourself.<br/><br/>The Quickstart Guide walks you through connecting your first MCP server.<br/><br/>And when you’re ready to explore more, head over to the tutorials section in the docs — it has step-by-step guides and short video demos to show you how to connect to a variety of MCP servers.<br/><br/>And don't forget to join the community to see what others are building, ask questions, or to simply connect.<br/><br/>Newer postFinetuning Toolshim Models for Tool CallingOlder postHow to Vibe Code Responsibly (with Goose)<br/><br/>* What Is MCP in Plain English?<br/>* Who Are The Players?<br/>* How Do They Communicate?<br/>* Here's An Analogy<br/>* Your Turn<br/><br/>Quick Links<br/><br/>* Install Goose<br/>* Extensions<br/><br/>Community<br/><br/>* Spotlight<br/>* Discord<br/>* YouTube<br/>* LinkedIn<br/>* Twitter / X<br/>* BlueSky<br/>* Nostr<br/><br/>More<br/><br/>* Blog<br/>* GitHub<br/><br/>Copyright © 2025 Block, Inc. |

Development<br/><br/># 4 Things You Need to Know Before Using Goose<br/><br/>April 23, 2025 · 5 min read<br/><br/>Ebony Louis<br/><br/>Ebony Louis<br/><br/>Developer Advocate<br/><br/>blog cover<br/><br/>So you’ve heard about Goose. Maybe you saw a livestream, someone on your team mentioned it, or you just stumbled into our corner of the internet while trying to automate your dev setup. Either way—love that for you.<br/><br/>Goose is a local, open source AI agent that can automate tasks, interact with your codebase, and connect to a growing ecosystem of tools. But before you hit install, here are four things you should know to get the most out of it.<br/><br/>---<br/><br/>## So Wait—What _Is_ Goose, Actually?​<br/><br/>Goose is an **MCP client**.<br/><br/>That means it connects to tools and data through something called the **Model Context Protocol (MCP)**—an open standard that makes it possible for AI agents to interact with external systems through natural language. If you’ve used Claude Desktop, Windsurf, Agent mode in VS Code or Cursor you’ve already used an MCP client, even if you didn’t realize it.<br/><br/>Here’s what makes Goose different:<br/><br/>* It runs **locally**, not in someone else’s cloud<br/>* You **bring your own LLM**, allowing you to use the one that works best for you<br/>* You can **add new capabilities**, using open-source MCP servers<br/><br/>Think of it less like “an AI assistant” and more like “your personal automation toolkit.” You decide which LLM to use, what tools it should have access to, and what tasks it can perform. You're not locked in; you're in charge.<br/><br/>---<br/><br/>## 1\. Pick the Right LLM​<br/><br/>Goose doesn’t bundle in an LLM. You bring your own LLM. That means you get to choose what kind of model works best for you, whether it’s a fancy hosted one like Claude or Gemini, or something more private and local like Ollama.<br/><br/>But heads up: not every model is created equal, especially when it comes to privacy, performance, or how much they charge you per token. If you're just exploring, a cloud-hosted LLM with a free tier is a great place to start. But if you’re working with sensitive data or just don’t want to send things off to a third-party server, local is the way to go.<br/><br/>Either way, Goose gives you the flexibility.<br/><br/>That said, if you’re looking for the best performance with Goose right now, Anthropic's Claude 3.5 Sonnet and OpenAI's GPT-4o (2024-11-20) are recommended, as they currently offer the strongest support for tool calling.<br/><br/>Curious how other models stack up? Check out the Community-Inspired Benchmark Leaderboard to see how your favorite model performs with Goose.<br/><br/>And if you’re still deciding, here’s the full list of available LLM providers.<br/><br/>---<br/><br/>## 2\. Understand What MCP Servers Are​<br/><br/>Here’s where things get fun. Goose is a client that speaks **MCP**. MCP is what makes it possible to talk to other apps and tools _as part of your prompt_. Want to read emails, check GitHub issues, run an automated test, or scrape a webpage? That’s where MCP servers come in.<br/><br/>Each server gives Goose a new ability.<br/><br/>The real question is: _what do you want Goose to be able to do?_ If there's a server for it, you can probably make it happen. And yes, there's an entire directory of MCP servers where you can search by tool, downloads, you name it.<br/><br/>---<br/><br/>## 3\. There _Can_ Be Costs​<br/><br/>Goose itself? Totally free and open source. 🎉 But your LLM provider might not be as generous.<br/><br/>Most models give you a free tier to play around with, but if you're doing anything intensive or using it often, you’ll eventually run into rate limits or token charges. That’s normal but it can sneak up on you if you’re not expecting it.<br/><br/>To help you manage this, there is a Handling Rate Limits Guide that you can check out.<br/><br/>---<br/><br/>## 4\. Tap Into the Community​<br/><br/>This part matters more than most people realize.<br/><br/>Goose has an entire community behind it—folks building, exploring, breaking things (and fixing them), and sharing everything they learn along the way. We hang out on Discord, we answer questions in GitHub Discussions, and we host livestreams every week to show off what Goose can do and how to make it do more.<br/><br/>There’s:<br/><br/>* **Goosing Around** – casual deep dives where we build in public<br/>* **Wild Goose Case** – showcasing cool community projects<br/>* **Great Goose Off** \- same task, same time limit, but different prompts, MCP servers, and strategies<br/><br/>You’ll find those livestreams on our YouTube channel, and upcoming ones on the Discord calendar. Plus, if you prefer documentation, the Goose docs and blog are constantly being updated with new guides, tips, and tutorials.<br/><br/>---<br/><br/>If you've got those four things: a performant LLM, the right MCP servers, a basic understanding of LLM cost, and a place to ask questions, you're more than ready to Goose.<br/><br/>Now, head over to the Quickstart Guide and get started.<br/><br/>Oh and when you get to the Tic-Tac-Toe game, I’ll bet you 10 Goosebucks you won’t beat the bot.<br/><br/>Newer postA Recipe for Success: Cooking Up Repeatable Agentic WorkflowsOlder postHow One Contribution Can Spark Many Wins<br/><br/>* So Wait—What _Is_ Goose, Actually?<br/>* 1\. Development<br/><br/># Community-Inspired Benchmarking: The Goose Vibe Check<br/><br/>March 31, 2025 · 20 min read<br/><br/>Alice Hau<br/><br/>Alice Hau<br/><br/>Machine Learning Engineer<br/><br/>blog cover<br/><br/>We've been measuring Goose's performance with various AI models, including a variety of popular open-source models that can run locally on consumer hardware (RTX 4080, Mac M-series). We understand that many in our community value a fully open-source, local experience without relying on cloud services.<br/><br/>This blog shares our findings comparing open-source models against their closed counterparts, highlighting both current performance gaps and paths for future improvement. Our benchmark is still in its early stages, but we wanted to release it as a starting point for distinguishing models that exhibit stronger agentic capabilities by their ability to pilot Goose (distinct from reasoning or other capabilities often captured in other popular benchmarks).<br/><br/>Our evaluations are inspired by grassroots efforts we've seen in communities like r/LocalLlama. If you've spent time there, you’ve probably seen enthusiasts crowdsource model performance on standard tasks like "build a flappy bird game" or create a rotating hexagon with a bouncing ball" to quickly compare model performance.<br/><br/>These community evals aren't the rigorous, peer-reviewed benchmarks that research labs publish in academic papers. However, they help provide quick, intuitive assessments of capabilities across different models and versions.<br/><br/>In this spirit, we're introducing our **Goose Vibe Check** leaderboard.<br/><br/>Thank you to the Ollama team for their help and support in our experimentation contributing to this blog! We used Ollama’s structured outputs feature to enable our toolshim implementation (more below) and their recently released context length parameter override to enable testing on longer model performance across different parameter sizes. In the 15-32B category, we see particularly impressive results from models like qwen2.5-coder:32b (0.80) and qwq (0.77). The chart also highlights the performance gap between models with native tool calling capabilities versus those requiring toolshim implementation (shown with dotted lines), a gap which appears consistent across all size categories. This suggests that native tool calling capabilities significantly impact performance on agentic tasks. With targeted improvements in tool calling capabilities, larger open models could potentially close the performance gap with closed-source alternatives in agentic settings._<br/><br/>Token Usage vs Scores<br/><br/>> _This scatterplot shows Claude models achieving top scores (0.9+) regardless of token usage, while open source models like qwen2.5-coder:32b perform well with moderate token consumption. Toolshimmed models consistently score lower, suggesting the toolshims are not very effective at closing the gap in native tool support between models. Higher token consumption up to a point appears to generally improve performance._<br/><br/>Tool Calls vs Scores<br/><br/>> _Models with either too few or excessive tool calls score lower, indicating effective tool utilization - not just frequency - correlates with improved performance. Toolshimmed models for the most part invoke fewer tool calls, suggesting that the toolshims are not sufficient in their current implementation to make models effective at correctly calling the right tools._<br/><br/>## Key Results​<br/><br/>1. **Closed models currently lead**: Closed source models like Claude and GPT models still generally lead open source alternatives in agentic tasks.<br/>2. **Promising open challengers**: Models like the Qwen series and DeepSeek-v3 show significant promise among open source alternatives, but they have not yet reached the consistency and reliability of closed models across all tasks.<br/>3. **Token efficiency matters**: Some open models can achieve good performance while using fewer tokens, which can translate to faster task completion times and potentially lower cost. Claude-3-7-sonnet exhibits strong performance alongside claude-3-5-sonnet-2, but at much greater token usage.<br/>4. **Tool calling is crucial but not as reliable in open source models today**: Effective tool calling remains a significant differentiator in agentic model performance. Open source models still struggle with generating structured tool calls reliably, limiting their effectiveness on complex tasks.<br/>5. **More comprehensive and complex eval tasks are needed to further stratify the top performers:** Our current evaluation suite, consisting of only eight tasks (ran 3x), may be too limited to effectively differentiate top-performing models. Several models clustered around similar scores in the .77-.81 range, likely due to the simplicity of the tasks, which require minimal complex reasoning. Expanding the evaluations to include more sophisticated tasks would provide further stratification and allow the models to better showcase their more or less advanced capabilities.<br/><br/>## Approach and Methodology​<br/><br/>We developed a compact suite of well-scoped evaluations to establish current performance baselines. While the tasks are relatively simple, they already meaningfully stratify model performance. Unlike benchmarks that focus primarily on text generation (e.g., question answering, code generation), our evaluations emphasize **tool calling capabilities** — a core component of what makes Goose a powerful agent.<br/><br/>Tool calling enables models to interact with MCP extensions and make API calls, expanding Goose's functionality beyond the base models. In many cases, tasks required multiple chained tool calls to reach completion. For instance, modifying a file involves finding it in your filesystem, viewing its contents, and then updating it. Each step must be executed correctly to complete the task effectively.<br/><br/>### Evaluation Suites​<br/><br/>Our evaluations are defined in the Goose repository (PRs welcome to add additional evals!) and are grouped into two categories:<br/><br/>#### Core Suite​<br/><br/>These evals focus on certain tasks fundamental to developer workflows:<br/><br/>* **Create a file**: Generate and save a new file<br/>* **List files**: Access and display directory contents<br/>* **Developer Search/Replace**: Search through a large file and make several replacements<br/><br/>#### Vibes Suite​<br/><br/>Designed as a "vibe check", these tasks quickly reveal how well models perform with Goose on a broad variety of tasks. Some, like the Flappy Bird and Goose Wiki tasks are straightforwardly visually inspectable, making it easy to eyeball outputs across models:<br/><br/>* **Blog summary**: Fetch a blog post and summarize key points<br/>* **Flappy Bird**: Implement the game in Python 2D<br/>* **Goose Wiki**: Create a Wikipedia-style webpage about Goose<br/>* **Restaurant research**: Search for the best Sichuanese restaurants in NYC's East Village<br/>* **Squirrel census**: Perform data analysis on a CSV file<br/><br/>This initial set of evaluations represents a carefully curated selection of manually designed tasks, chosen to highlight key strengths and weaknesses of models when integrated with Goose. However, this is just the beginning! Our goal is to continuously expand the Goosebench evaluation suite with high-quality, targeted tasks that provide deeper insights into model performance with Goose.<br/><br/>### Evaluation Methodology​<br/><br/>Each model was tested on the above **8 tasks, with 3 runs per task**, (totaling **24 runs per model**):<br/><br/>* Each evaluation consisted of a single turn prompt to Goose. While this benchmark focuses on single turn execution, future evaluations may assess multi-turn interactions and iterative improvement<br/>* Goose was required to autonomously complete the task using tool execution loops without user intervention<br/>* If Goose halted execution and asked the user for more guidance (e.g., "I am going to write the following contents to the file. Should I continue?"), this was considered the end of task completion. In such cases, Goose may not have successfully completed the task as measured by our evaluation framework, even if it was on the right track.<br/>* To account for output variability, each evaluation was run three times per model, allowing multiple chances for success.<br/><br/>### Scoring and Evaluation Criteria​<br/><br/>We calculate each model's leaderboard score by averaging its performance across all evaluation tasks. For each task, we run the model three times and normalize each run's score to a 0-1 scale. The model's task score is the average of these three runs. The final leaderboard score is the average of all task scores for that model.<br/><br/>Each evaluation is scored on a mix of criteria tailored to the specific task:<br/><br/>1. **Tool Call Execution**: Did the model make the correct tool calls to complete the task?<br/>2. **LLM as a Judge** (where applicable): Some evaluations used GPT-4o to assess response quality on a 0-2 scale. In these cases, we generated 3 GPT-4o assessments, took the most common score among them, and ran a fourth assessment if needed to break a tie to get the final score.  <br/>   * 0 points: Incorrect or fundamentally flawed  <br/>   * 1 point: Partially correct, but with issues  <br/>   * 2 points: Fully correct and well executed<br/>3. **Task Specific Criteria**: Different tasks required different checks, such as:  <br/>   * Correct output formatting (e.g., markdown, output to file)  <br/>   * Expected answers (e.g., correct insights in data analysis)  <br/>   * Valid implementation (e.g., valid Python code)<br/><br/>Some evaluations, like code execution or file creation, have clear pass/fail criteria, similar to unit tests. Others, such as blog summarization or restaurant research, require qualitative judgment rather than strict correctness. To assess both objective and open-ended tasks, we combine task-specific criteria, tool call verification, and (where applicable) LLM as a judge scoring.<br/><br/>To assess both objective and open-ended tasks, we combine task-specific criteria, tool call verification, and (where applicable) LLM-as-a-judge scoring. This approach maintains rigor where correctness is well-defined while allowing for nuanced evaluation of subjective outputs.<br/><br/>Our goal is to provide a directional signal of model performance rather than absolute accuracy, balancing concrete and qualitative criteria.<br/><br/>Additionally, we tracked:<br/><br/>1. **Token Efficiency**: Measures total tokens used in successful runs, providing insight into model efficiency and inference speed.<br/>2. **Duration**: Time to execute the task. This is not reflected in the leaderboard as it is significantly affected by differences across model inference providers and hardware.<br/><br/>### Manual Inspection and Observations of Results​<br/><br/>We manually inspected a handful of results to assess quality. Given the scale (768 total runs across 32 models), full manual validation of every evaluation run was infeasible. Key takeaways from our inspections:<br/><br/>* LLM-as-a-judge was reliable at identifying fully incorrect answers (0 points), but distinguishing between 1 and 2 points was more subjective.<br/>* Some tasks (e.g., blog summarization, restaurant searches) lacked automated factual verification. The evaluation framework could confirm whether a tool was called (e.g., web search executed) and the LLM judge could assess the instruction following to some degree, but our system overall had no way of verifying if the responses were factually correct.<br/>* Tool execution failures were a key source of performance variation, highlighting the importance of agentic capabilities in real-world AI tasks. A model might generate the correct output in chat, but if it fails to subsequently execute the right tools—such as writing the output to the right file as instructed by the user—the task is incomplete. This underscores the need for models to reliably perform multi-step actions autonomously, not just generate accurate responses.<br/><br/>## Technical Challenges with Open Models​<br/><br/>### Context Length Limitations​<br/><br/>A key limitation we encountered early on in our experimentation was the default context length in Ollama's OpenAI-compatible endpoint (2048 tokens), which proved insufficient for most interactive agent scenarios.<br/><br/>Our system prompt alone consumes about 1,000 tokens, leaving limited space for user queries, context, and tool responses. This restriction hampers the model's ability to manage long-running or complex tasks without losing essential context. While quantization (e.g., many Ollama models default to 4-bit) can reduce memory usage, it can also degrade performance.<br/><br/>However, we did not extensively explore the impact of different quantization levels. Fortunately, during our work, Ollama introduced an override that allowed us to increase the context length, helping to mitigate this limitation in our experiments.<br/><br/>### Tool Calling Inconsistencies Across Models​<br/><br/>Different models have varying expectations for tool calling formats. For instance, Ollama requires JSON, while others like Functionary use XML. This lack of standardization poses integration challenges for inference providers, who must adapt the tool calling mechanisms for each model.<br/><br/>We observed performance fluctuations based on the model host and input/output formatting, highlighting the need for standardized tool calling formats in model training. For models without native tool calling capabilities, we developed a "toolshim"—an interpretive layer that translates a model's output into the appropriate tool calls.<br/><br/>This approach enables models like DeepSeek and Gemma to perform basic tool actions, though performance remains limited. None of the models configured with the toolshim greater than a 41% success rate in our experiments. Future improvements may focus on fine-tuning these shims for better handling of agentic tasks, helping to reduce inconsistencies across models in tool call generation.<br/><br/>### “Toolshims” to bridge the gap?​<br/><br/>We developed a "toolshim" as an experimental feature to enable models lacking native tool calling support (e.g., DeepSeek, Gemma3, Phi4) to interact with external tools. The toolshim pairs these models with a smaller, local model (e.g., mistral-nemo, qwen2.5-coder 7b), which is tasked with translating the primary model’s natural language responses into the appropriate tool calls for Goose to invoke. The local model is guided by Ollama’s structured outputs feature to enforce proper formatting for tool call generations.<br/><br/>However, this solution has limited performance due to:<br/><br/>* **Instruction-following limitations:** The smaller models used typically have less robust instruction-following ability especially for longer inputs, making them prone to inaccuracies when parsing the primary model's output into the correct tool calls. We also found the shim models to be quite sensitive to prompting.<br/>* **Structured output interference:** Ollama’s structured output feature influences the model’s token sampling process, where the output is impacted by the model’s fundamental ability to extract information and generate JSON appropriately.<br/><br/>Despite these challenges, there could be potential in fine-tuning these toolshim models to specifically optimize them for tool call generation. If you’d like to try out the toolshim, check out our documentation<br/><br/>## Practical Advice for Local Model Users​<br/><br/>For those running a local, open-source AI experience with Goose, here are some key recommendations based on our testing:<br/><br/>### Optimize Context Length​<br/><br/>Ensure your model has enough context length to avoid running out of space in the context window. For Ollama, you can adjust the context length via an environment variable:<br/><br/>```<br/>OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=28672 ollama serve<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>You can also set the context length as a parameter in Ollama by updating the Modlfile with your desired context length and running `ollama create`.<br/><br/>### Be Aware of Quantization Levels​<br/><br/>Different quantization levels (4-bit, 8-bit, and 16-bit) have distinct impacts on performance:<br/><br/>* **4-bit:** Offers maximum compression with minimal memory requirements but may degrade quality.<br/>* **8-bit:** A balanced option for most consumer hardware, providing good performance and reasonable quality.<br/>* **16-bit:** Higher quality but requires significantly more memory, which may limit performance on lower-end hardware.<br/><br/>Ollama defaults to 4-bit quantization in most cases, but for tasks requiring more complex reasoning or tool usage, testing with higher quantization levels (e.g., 8-bit) may improve performance.<br/><br/>### Prompting Matters for Smaller Models​<br/><br/>Smaller models are more sensitive to prompt variations and often require more explicit instructions due to their limited capacity to infer. To achieve optimal performance, tasks may need to be broken down further, reducing ambiguity and limiting the range of possible responses.<br/><br/>### Hardware Considerations​<br/><br/>We ran these models with a variety of inference providers (local and hosted) and hardware configurations including Apple M1, NVIDIA RTX 4080, NVIDIA RTX 4090, and NVIDIA H100\. Due to the mix of hardware, we did not include measurements of task duration in the benchmark given the expected variability in inference performance driven by the underlying hardware.<br/><br/>#### GPU Backends​<br/><br/>Depending on your hardware, different GPU acceleration backends offer varying levels of performance:<br/><br/>* **CUDA (NVIDIA GPUs)**: Currently offers the best performance and compatibility for running LLMs locally. Most open models and inference frameworks are optimized for CUDA first.<br/>* **Metal (Apple Silicon)**: Provides good acceleration on Mac devices with M-series chips. While not as fast as high-end NVIDIA GPUs, recent optimization work has made Metal increasingly viable for running 7B-13B models.<br/>* **ROCm (AMD GPUs)**: Support is improving but still lags behind CUDA. If you have a compatible AMD GPU, you may expect to see some performance limitations and compatibility issues with certain models and quantization methods.<br/><br/>#### CPU/GPU Memory Management​<br/><br/>Ollama helps distribute model layers across CPU and GPU memory, allowing you to run larger models than would fit entirely in your GPU VRAM. However, be aware of:<br/><br/>* **Data movement overhead**: When a model doesn't fit entirely in GPU memory, constant data movement between CPU and GPU can significantly impact performance<br/>* **GPU utilization**: Models that fit entirely in GPU memory will perform dramatically better than those that require CPU offloading<br/><br/>### Considering Cloud-Hosted Open Models?​<br/><br/>If using a cloud service like OpenRouter to try larger open-weight models (e.g., LLaMA 3 70B or Qwen), be aware that performance may vary depending on which hosted inference provider you're using.<br/><br/>Different providers might:<br/><br/>* Quantize models on the backend without clear disclosure<br/>* Implement different integration patterns that affect model performance, especially with tool calling<br/>* Have different hardware configurations affecting speed and reliability<br/><br/>We recommend experimenting with different hosted inference providers to see which works best for your specific use cases. OpenRouter for example lets you specify the provider you want to route your requests to.<br/><br/>## Run Your Own Benchmarks​<br/><br/>We encourage the community to conduct their own benchmarks with various hardware setups and configurations to help deepen our understanding of how Goose performs across different setups. We also welcome contributions of additional evals to GooseBench to broaden our coverage.<br/><br/>We are currently cleaning up our code and working on some quality of life improvements to make the process of running evals and reproducing these results more streamlined, and will share those when ready (next few weeks)!<br/><br/>Special thanks to our contributors, Zaki and Marcelle, for their work on GooseBench, which enabled this experimentation.<br/><br/>## Future Work​<br/><br/>As AI capabilities continue to evolve, we aim to systematically expand our evaluation framework to capture a broader range of use cases. We hope to benchmark models on a wider swath of consumer-grade hardware to better understand system requirements, execution times, and the impact of different quantization levels on performance.<br/><br/>We also plan to introduce vision-oriented evaluations, particularly for multimodal models with Goose. These will assess image processing, multimodal reasoning, and visual tool interactions, helping us measure how well models integrate and perform across different modalities.<br/><br/>In addition, we seek to develop evaluations tailored to non-developer workflows and tasks. This will provide insights into how Goose and AI models can serve a wider range of users beyond technical audiences.<br/><br/>Finally, we see value in testing long-context retention and multi-turn interactions to evaluate model performance in complex, sustained conversations.<br/><br/>## Result Eval Examples​<br/><br/>### Flappy Bird​<br/><br/>For runs that successfully created a working flappy bird game with pygame, here are the gifs of playing the games:<br/><br/>### claude-3-5-haiku<br/><br/>Slide 1<br/><br/>Slide 2<br/><br/>Slide 3<br/><br/>Slide 4<br/><br/>Slide 5<br/><br/>Slide 6<br/><br/>Slide 7<br/><br/>Slide 8<br/><br/>Slide 9<br/><br/>Slide 10<br/><br/>Slide 11<br/><br/>Slide 12<br/><br/>### Wiki Pages​<br/><br/>For runs that successfully created an index.html for the Wiki page task, here’s what the rendered outputs look like: Wiki pages Missing results are for models that did not successfully write to an index.html file. | Building a Personal AI Factory (July 2025 snapshot) | https://www.john-rush.com/posts/ai-20250701.html | * home<br/>* about<br/><br/># Building a Personal AI Factory (July 2025 snapshot)<br/><br/>AI Factory<br/><br/>_Published: July 1, 2025_<br/><br/>## Overview<br/><br/>I keep several claude code windows open, each on its own git-worktree. o3 and sonnet 4 create plans, sonnet 3.7 or sonnet 4 execute the plan, and o3 checks the results against the original ask. Any issues found are fed back into the plan template and the code is regenerated. The factory improves itself.<br/><br/>Read on to see what might be useful for you.<br/><br/>## Guiding Principle – Fix Inputs, Not Outputs<br/><br/>When something goes wrong, I don’t hand-patch the generated code. I don’t argue with claude. Instead, I adjust the plan, the prompts, or the agent mix so the next run is correct by construction.<br/><br/>If you know Factorio you know it’s all about building a factory that can produce itself. If not, picture a top-down sandbox where conveyor belts and machines endlessly craft parts because the factory must grow. Do the same thing with AI agents: build a factory of agents that can produce code, verify it, and improve themselves over time.<br/><br/>## Basic day to day workflow - building the factory<br/><br/>My main interface is claude code. It’s my computer now. I also have a local mcp which runs Goose and o3\. Goose only because I’ve already got it setup to use the models hosted in our Azure OpenAI subscription. Looking to improve this at some point, but it works for now.<br/><br/>### Step 1: Planning<br/><br/>I’ll give a high level task to claude code, which calls over to o3 to generate a plan. o3 is a good planner and can ask a bunch of good questions to clarify the job to be done. I then have it write out a `<task>-plan.md` file with both my original ask and an implementation plan.<br/><br/>### Step 2: Execution<br/><br/>First, sonnet 4 reads the plan, verifies it, and turns it into a task list. Next claude code execute the plan, either with sonnet 3.7 or sonnet 4 depending on the complexity of the task. Because most of my day-to-day is in clojure I tend to use sonnet 4 to get the parens right. One important instruction is to have claude write commits as it goes for each task step. This way either claude or I can revert to a previous state if something goes wrong.<br/><br/>### Step 3: Verification → Feedback into Inputs<br/><br/>Once the code is generated, I have sonnet 4 verify the code against the original plan. Then I have o3 verify the code against the original plan and original ask. o3 is uncompromising. Claude wants to please, so will keep unnecessary backwards compatibility code in place. o3 will call that out and ask for it to be removed. Claude also tends to add “lint ignore flags” to the code which o3 will also call out. Having both models verify the code catches issues and saves me back and forth with claude.<br/><br/>Any issue sonnet 4 or o3 finds gets baked back into the plan template, not fixed inline.<br/><br/>Git worktrees let me open concurrent claude code instances and build multiple features at once. I still merge manually, but I’m no longer babysitting a single agent.<br/><br/>## Why Inputs Trump Outputs<br/><br/>* Outputs are disposable; plans and prompts compound.<br/>* Debugging at the source scales across every future task.<br/>* It transforms agents from code printers into self-improving colleagues.<br/><br/>Example: an agent once wrote code that would load an entire CSV into memory. I made it switch to streaming and had the agent write instructions to the plan to always use streaming for CSVs. Now, my plan checker flags any code that doesn’t use streaming for CSVs, and I don’t have to remember this in every PR review. The factory improves itself.<br/><br/>## Scaling the factory<br/><br/>I’ve started to encode more complex workflows, where I have specific agents (behind mcps) for building specific tasks.<br/><br/>One MCP will sweep all the clojure code generated and then apply our local style rules. These rules are part of the instructions for the original plan and agent but often the generated code will have style issues. Especially once claude gets in the lint/test/debug cycle. This focused agent means we have tighter behavior and can apply our style rules consistently.<br/><br/>I’ve started doing this for internal libraries as well. It’s good at looking at generated code and replacing things like retries and `Thread/sleep` with our retry library.<br/><br/>I’m also building out a collection of these small agents. Each one can take a small specific task, and by composing them together I can build more complex workflows. For example, I can take an api doc, and a set of internally defined business cases and have a composition of agents build integrations, tests, and documentation for the api. This is a powerful way to build out features and integrations without having to do all the work by hand.<br/><br/>You don’t get there in one big step. Here’s the secret sauce: **iterate the inputs**<br/><br/>It’s essentially free to fire off a dozen attempts at a task - so I do. All agents run in parallel. When one fails, stalls, or lacks context, I feed that lesson into the next iteration. I resist the urge to fix outputs, instead I fix the inputs.<br/><br/>That loop is the factory: the code itself is disposable; the instructions and agents are the real asset.<br/><br/>## Next up<br/><br/>I’m working on a few things to improve the factory:<br/><br/>* Better overall coordination of the agents. I tend to kick things off manually, but I want to have a more automated way to manage the workflow and dependencies between agents.<br/>* Aligning our business docs with the agents. Changing the information we capture to be at a higher level of abstraction so that the agents can use it more effectively. This means moving away from low level implementation details and focusing on use cases.<br/>* More complex workflows. I’ve been able to build some pretty complex workflows with the current setup, but I want to push it further. This means more agents, more coordination, and more complex interactions between them.<br/>* Maximize token usage across providers. I’m pretty limited by bedrock’s token limits especially for sonnet 4\. Going to need to be able to switch between the claude max plan and bedrock w/out interruption.<br/><br/>## Wrapping Up<br/><br/>That’s where my factory sits today: good enough to ship code while I refill my coffee, not yet good enough to bump me off the payroll. Constraints will shift, but the core principle remains: **fix inputs, not outputs**. |

</details>

Re-wired the ingestion worker to use Goose + Claude Code directly instead of the missing `github-index` recipe:

• After cloning the repo the worker now runs  
  `goose --provider claude-code --loader dir=<repo> … --out system-map.json`  
  which asks Claude Code to emit a JSON “system-map”.  
• Removed the old fallback recipe logic.  
• No other flow changed—on success the map is persisted and the `project.indexed` event fires exactly as before.

Just restart the worker (`npm run worker`) after you’ve installed/​configured Goose with the `claude-code` provider and you’ll get end-to-end indexing again.

Development<br/><br/># Resolving CI Issues with Goose: A Practical Walkthrough<br/><br/>December 11, 2024 · 4 min read<br/><br/>Dalton Turner<br/><br/>Dalton Turner<br/><br/>Software Engineer<br/><br/>CI<br/><br/>Running into Continuous Integration (CI) failures in pull requests can be quite frustrating but they happen very often. In this post, we leverage the GitHub CLI (`gh`) using Goose to simplify your CI debugging process, fetch detailed information about failed CI runs and annotations directly from GitHub, and even apply fixes directly.<br/><br/>Goose Beta Version<br/><br/>This post was written about a beta version of Goose and the commands and flow may have changed.<br/><br/>## Getting Started​<br/><br/>Before diving in, ensure you have the necessary tools set up.<br/><br/>### 1\. Install and Authenticate GitHub CLI (`gh`)​<br/><br/>You'll need the GitHub CLI `gh` to enable Goose's access to CI check run details.<br/><br/>```<br/>brew install gh<br/>gh auth login<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>Follow the prompts to authenticate your account.<br/><br/>### 2\. Configure Goose​<br/><br/>Ensure Goose is configured and ready to interact with your repository and local tools. Specifically, you will need to configure a goose profile with the GitHub toolkit.<br/><br/>Update your `profiles.yaml` file in `~/.config/goose` with the necessary toolkits:<br/><br/>```<br/>my-profile:<br/>  provider: anthropic<br/>  processor: claude-3-5-sonnet<br/>  accelerator: claude-3-5-sonnet<br/>  moderator: truncate<br/>  toolkits:<br/>    - name: developer<br/>      requires: \{}<br/>    - name: github<br/>      requires: \{}<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>Start a session with the profile:<br/><br/>```<br/>goose session start --profile my-profile<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>If the profile’s toolkits are not correctly configured, Goose might fail to access `gh` commands.<br/><br/>## Resolving CI Failures with Goose​<br/><br/>Once everything is set up, we can now use Goose to tackle CI issues with the following steps:<br/><br/>### Step 1: Fetch CI Failure Details​<br/><br/>Ask Goose to retrieve information about the CI failures for a specific PR.<br/><br/>**Example Request:**<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>Can you tell me about the CI failures on PR #11111 in the organization/repo repository? The check run ID is 123456.<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>You can access a check run ID by clicking on a PR’s checks tab and selecting a failure. The ID will be available in the URL.<br/><br/>**Goose's Workflow:**<br/><br/>Goose will use the `gh` CLI to check run information and provide a detailed summary of the issues. Goose uses the GitHub CLI to:<br/><br/>* Fetch details about failed CI runs, including logs and annotations.<br/>* Provide a clear and actionable summary of issues.<br/><br/>**Example Command Goose Runs:**<br/><br/>```<br/>gh api -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" /repos/<owner>/<repo>/check-runs/<check-run-id>/annotations<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>**Example Goose Output:**<br/><br/>```<br/>Here are the details for Check Run ID 123456:<br/><br/>**Name**: CI-Build-All  <br/>**Status**: completed  <br/>**Conclusion**: failure  <br/><br/>**Annotations Summary:**  <br/>1. **ModuleA Test Failure**  <br/>   File: `ModuleATests`  <br/>   Line: 35  <br/>   Error: Mismatched parameter order in function call.  <br/><br/>2. **ModuleB Test Failure**  <br/>   File: `ModuleBTests`  <br/>   Line: 64  <br/>   Error: Unexpected nil value encountered during initialization.  <br/><br/>3. **ModuleC Test Failure**  <br/>   File: `ModuleCTests`  <br/>   Line: 98  <br/>   Error: Type mismatch in returned value. Expected 'String', found 'Int'.  <br/><br/>```<br/><br/>### Step 2: Request Fixes from Goose​<br/><br/>Once Goose provides the failure details, ask it to resolve the issues directly.<br/><br/>Example Request:<br/><br/>```<br/>Can you fix these issues and stage the changes so I can review them? Do not add unnecessary code comments.<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>**What Goose Does:**<br/><br/>* Applies fixes based on error messages.<br/>* Stages changes for review.<br/><br/>**Example Goose Response:**<br/><br/>```<br/>I have fixed the following files and staged them:<br/><br/>- `ModuleATests`: Corrected the order of parameters in the function call.  <br/>- `ModuleBTests`: Resolved the unexpected nil value encountered during initialization.  <br/>- `ModuleCTests`: Adjusted the type mismatch in the returned value.  <br/><br/>You can now review the staged changes.<br/><br/>```<br/><br/>### Step 3: Review the Changes​<br/><br/>Carefully review the staged changes to ensure they address the issues correctly and avoid unintended modifications.<br/><br/>**Things to Check:**<br/><br/>* No unnecessary comments (e.g., // Fix xyz).<br/>* No alterations to unrelated parts of the code.<br/><br/>If needed, clean up or re-stage the changes before committing.<br/><br/>## Benefits of Using Goose​<br/><br/>Using Goose to resolve CI issues streamlines your workflow by:<br/><br/>* identifying issues and applying fixes with minimal manual effort.<br/>* integrating with tools like the GitHub CLI to validate changes.<br/>* handling repetitive CI debugging tasks while you focus on code quality.<br/><br/>Goose allows you to resolve CI failures efficiently, ensuring confidence in your workflow while reducing the effort required for debugging and testing.<br/><br/>Try it out, and let Goose handle the heavy lifting of CI debugging for you!<br/><br/>Newer postIntroducing codename gooseOlder postConnecting AI Agents to Your Systems with MCP<br/><br/>* Getting Started  <br/>   * 1\. | Embedding migrations - pressly/goose | https://pressly.github.io/goose/blog/2021/embed-sql-migrations/ | Skip to content <br/><br/>logo <br/><br/> pressly/goose <br/><br/> Embedding migrations <br/><br/> Initializing search<br/><br/> pressly/goose <br/><br/>* Getting Started<br/>* Documentation<br/>* Blog<br/><br/>logo  pressly/goose <br/><br/> pressly/goose <br/><br/>* Getting Started  <br/> Getting Started  <br/>   * Installation<br/>* Documentation  <br/> Documentation  <br/>   * Concepts  <br/>    Concepts  <br/>         * SQL file annotations  <br/>   * Library  <br/>    Library  <br/>         * Goose provider  <br/>   * CLI  <br/>    CLI  <br/>         * Commands  <br/>         * Environment variables  <br/>   * Guides  <br/>    Guides  <br/>         * Custom store<br/>* Blog  <br/> Blog  <br/>   * Archive  <br/>    Archive  <br/>         * 2024  <br/>         * 2023  <br/>         * 2022  <br/>         * 2021  <br/>   * Categories  <br/>    Categories  <br/>         * Blog  <br/>         * ClickHouse  <br/>         * General  <br/>         * Go migrations  <br/>         * Package  <br/>         * SQL migrations  <br/>         * Testing<br/><br/> Table of contents <br/>* Embedding migrations<br/>* But why?<br/>* Gotchas<br/>* Try it out!<br/><br/> Back to index <br/><br/>Mike Fridman   **Mike Fridman**   <br/> Maintainer <br/><br/>* Metadata  <br/>   * Aug 21, 2021  <br/>   * inBlog, Go migrations<br/><br/># Embedding migrations<br/><br/>## Embedding migrations<br/><br/>Go continues to be boring while sprinkling quality of life features. One of the recent additions was the ability to embed files at compile time. Click here forgo1.16 release notes.<br/><br/>Sine many users compile `goose` themselves, this new embed feature paves the way for embedding SQL files directly into the `goose` binary. This was _already_ possible with existing tools, however, now that embedding is part of the standard library it's never been easier to offer this feature.<br/><br/>## **But why?**<br/><br/>We'll save "why would I compile `goose` myself?" for another post, instead we'll focus on why embedding files is an improvement to existing workflows.<br/><br/>A typical workflow looks something like this:<br/><br/>1. Developer introduces new SQL migration file<br/>2. File gets merged to `main` and a `goose` binary is built<br/>3. The binary _along with SQL files_ is copied into a docker container<br/>4. The docker container is run as a singleton against the database before the application starts up<br/><br/>One of the cumbersome things about this workflow is that the `goose` binary and the migration files need to be shipped together and the directory structure has to be maintained.<br/><br/>But now that `goose` natively supports embedding files it simplifies the workflow. A `goose` binary is shipped without any file dependencies, i.e., the migration files are baked into the binary itself.<br/><br/>## **Gotchas**<br/><br/>We did not implement this in a backwards-compatible way, i.e., the feature is not guarded with build tags. Which means starting with v3.1.0 you must be on go1.16 and up.<br/><br/>For older `goose` versions you may still pinv3.0.1.<br/><br/>## **Try it out!**<br/><br/>Remember, the files to be embedded must be relative to the source file(s). Here is what our directory structure _might_ look like:<br/><br/>`.<br/>├── embed_example.sql<br/>├── go.mod<br/>├── go.sum<br/>└── internal<br/>    └── goose<br/>        ├── main.go<br/>        └── migrations<br/>            └── 00001_create_users_table.sql<br/>`<br/><br/>Here is a fully working example using an in-memory database (SQLite).<br/><br/>`` package main<br/><br/>import (<br/>    "database/sql"<br/>    "embed"<br/>    "log"<br/><br/>    _ "github.com/mattn/go-sqlite3"<br/>    "github.com/pressly/goose/v3"<br/>)<br/><br/>//go:embed migrations/*.sql<br/>var embedMigrations embed.FS // (1)<br/><br/>func main() \{<br/>    log.SetFlags(0)<br/>    db, err := sql.Open("sqlite3", "embed_example.sql")<br/>    if err != nil \{<br/>        log.Fatal(err)<br/>    \}<br/>    goose.SetDialect("sqlite3")<br/>    goose.SetBaseFS(embedMigrations) // (2)<br/><br/>    if err := goose.Up(db, "migrations"); err != nil \{ // (3)<br/>        panic(err)<br/>    \}<br/>    if err := goose.Version(db, "migrations"); err != nil \{<br/>        log.Fatal(err)<br/>    \}<br/>    rows, err := db.Query(`SELECT * FROM users`)<br/>    if err != nil \{<br/>        log.Fatal(err)<br/>    \}<br/>    var user struct \{<br/>        ID       int<br/>        Username string<br/>    \}<br/>    for rows.Next() \{<br/>        if err := rows.Scan(&user.ID, &user.Username); err != nil \{<br/>            log.Fatal(err)<br/>        \}<br/>        log.Println(user.ID, user.Username)<br/>    \}<br/>\}<br/> ``<br/><br/>1. This `//go:embed` is a special directive that tells the Go tooling to read files from the package directory or subdirectories at compile time and stores them in the a variable of type`embed.FS`.  <br/>    <br/>The `embed.FS` will store a read-only collection of \*.sql files.<br/>2. Pass the `embed.FS` variable to `goose`. This instructs `goose` to use the embedded filesystem instead of opening files from the underlying os.<br/>3. You still have to tell `goose` which directory contains the .sql files. This implementation allowed us to keep existing functions without having to change the function signature or add new functions.  <br/>    <br/>It is a drop-in feature that enables the caller to either use the os (as before) or use embedded filesystem without changing parts of their existing programs.<br/><br/>---<br/><br/>A sample repo can be found at mfridmn/goose-demo<br/><br/>From the root of the directory you can build the binary, and to prove it has no dependencies move it to your home directory and run the binary. This will create a embed\_example.sql file for sqlite database. Cool right?!<br/><br/>`go build -o goosey internal/goose/main.go<br/>mv goosey $HOME<br/>cd $HOME<br/>./goosey<br/>`<br/><br/>**Output:**<br/><br/>`OK    00001_create.sql<br/>goose: no migrations to run. current version: 1<br/>goose: version 1<br/>0 root<br/>1 goosey<br/>`<br/><br/> Back to top <br/><br/> Made with Material for MkDocs Insiders |

That “goose” binary on your PATH is the old Pressly SQL-migration tool, not the “codename-goose” CLI that talks to Claude Code.  
Because the wrong binary is picking up the call it chokes on flags such as ­­­`--provider`.

What you need to do

1  Install the right CLI (one-time)  
```bash
# if you already have Node 18+
npm i -g @block/codename-goose   # puts a `goose` shim in ~/.npm-global/bin
#  – or –
npx @block/codename-goose@latest install
```
(this is the agent-oriented Goose – you’ll see `goose configure` in its help)

2  Make sure it’s ahead of the SQL-Goose in `$PATH`  
```bash
# quick test – should show the provider list, not migration commands
goose --help | head
```

3  Configure Claude Code once so Goose can call it:  
```bash
GOOSE_PROVIDER=claude-code goose configure    # choose “Configure Providers”
```

4  Restart the worker  
```bash
npm run worker
```
You should now see:

```
→ generating system map with Goose + Claude Code
✅ System map generated at …/artifacts/<id>/system-map.json
```

If you still need the migration tool, rename it (`goose-sql`) so the two CLIs don’t clash.

That’s all – the ingestion pipeline will work as-is once the correct Goose CLI is on the PATH.

Two very different programs share the name `goose`.

1. `goose` (the **SQL-migration** utility from pressly/goose)  
2. `goose` (the **AI agent** CLI from Block/codename-goose that talks to Claude-Code)

Mission-Control’s Dashboard already shells out to # 2.  
The ingestion worker, however, just executes the first binary called “goose” it finds in `$PATH`.  
On your laptop that happens to be the SQL tool, so the run dies on flags like `--provider`.

How to fix it (pick one)

──────────────────────────────── Option A – rename the old binary
```bash
# Find both binaries
which -a goose
# e.g. /usr/local/bin/goose   <- SQL tool
#      ~/.npm-global/bin/goose <- AI agent (or wherever npm installs globals)

sudo mv /usr/local/bin/goose /usr/local/bin/goose-sql   # or delete it
hash -r                                                  # clear shell cache
```
Now any `goose …` call will pick up the AI agent.

──────────────────────────────── Option B – give the worker the exact path
Edit `worker/ingestionWorker.js` once:

```diff
-const GOOSE_CMD = process.env.GOOSE_CMD || 'goose'
+const GOOSE_CMD = process.env.GOOSE_CMD
+  || require.resolve('.bin/goose')   // AI-goose inside mission-control/node_modules
```
(or hard-code `/Users/…/.npm-global/bin/goose` if you prefer).  
Restart with `npm run worker`.

──────────────────────────────── Option C – call via npx (no global install needed)
Replace the `run(GOOSE_CMD …)` line with:
```js
await run('npx', ['--yes', '@block/codename-goose', ...gooseArgs])
```
This downloads the right CLI at call-time and bypasses any name clash.

After one of those changes:

```bash
npm run worker
# → generating system map with Goose + Claude Code
# ✅ System map generated … 🎉
```

The rest of the pipeline stays exactly the same—no changes needed in your Dashboard or PO interface.
